**Input:** naturals $n,d\ge1$, a fixed design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a data
vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a penalty $\tau^2\ge0$.

List all supports $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ in lexicographic order of their
length-$d$ indicator vectors, using $0<1$. For each $S$, let $V_S$ be the span
of the corresponding columns of $X$, compute $\widehat\mu_S=P_{V_S}y$, and
score

$$q_S:=n^{-1}\|y-\widehat\mu_S\|_2^2+\tau^2|S|.$$

Initialize the incumbent at the first support and scan the rest in order,
replacing it exactly when a strictly smaller score is found; on a tie retain the
earlier support. Return the selected support $\widehat S$ and fitted vector
$\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{BIC}}=\widehat\mu_{\widehat S}$. The candidate family is
finite by [[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], and the fitted-vector selection
is Borel measurable by [[lem-finite-support-projection-selection-is-borel]].
This is an exhaustive combinatorial procedure, not an efficiency guarantee.

vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a natural $s$ with $0\le s\le d$.

**Candidate supports:** list all subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ with
$|S|\le s$ in lexicographic order of their length-$d$ indicator vectors,
using $0<1$. This is a finite nonempty list because it contains $\varnothing$
and is contained in the finite power set of $\{1,\ldots,d\}$.

**Procedure:** for each candidate $S$, let $V_S$ be the span of the columns of
$X$ indexed by $S$ and compute $\widehat\mu_S=P_{V_S}y$. Compute its residual
score $q_S=\|y-\widehat\mu_S\|_2^2$. Initialize the incumbent at the first
candidate. Scan the remaining candidates in the stated order, replacing the
incumbent exactly when a strictly smaller score is found; retain the earlier
candidate on a tie. Return the selected support and its fitted vector
$\widehat\mu_s$.

Each $V_S$ is finite-dimensional, so the projections are defined by
[[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. The fitted-vector selection is Borel
measurable by [[lem-finite-support-projection-selection-is-borel]]. The procedure
performs a finite exhaustive support search; no computational-efficiency claim is
made.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: For $x=1$, the transformed statistic values are $T(e\cdot1)=1$ and $T(s\cdot1)=0$, so exactly one of the two group elements has value at least $T(1)$ and $p_0(1)=1/2$. read_units.claim_anchor:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=[0,1]$, let $\mathcal A$ be the countable-cocountable sigma-algebra, and define

$$P(A):=\begin{cases}0,&A\text{ is countable},\\1,&\Omega\setminus A\text{ is countable}.\end{cases}$$

For $U:=[0,1/2]$, take the uncountable class of functions $\mathcal F:=\{f_t:t\in U\}$ with $f_t(\omega):=\mathbf1_{\{t\}}(\omega)$. Every $f_t$ is measurable and $Pf_t=0$, but for one observation $Z(\omega)=\omega$,

$$\sup_{t\in U}|f_t(Z(\omega))-Pf_t|=\mathbf1_U(\omega),$$

which is not measurable because $U$ is neither countable nor cocountable.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: By [F1], $\Omega$ is uncountable. The empty set is at most countable, and complementation exchanges the countable and cocountable alternatives, so $\mathcal A$ contains the empty set and is complement-closed. For a sequence $(A_n)$ in $\mathcal A$, if every $A_n$ is countable then [A1] makes their union countable; otherwise some $A_j$ is cocountable, and $\Omega\setminus\bigcup_n A_n\subseteq\Omega\setminus A_j$ is countable by [F2]. Thus the union lies in $\mathcal A$ in either case, proving all sigma-algebra axioms in [F5]. The assignment $P$ is well-defined: a set and its complement cannot both be countable, since their union would make $\Omega$ countable. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Let $(A_n)$ be pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal A$. If every $A_n$ is countable, [A1] makes their union countable; then $P(\bigcup_nA_n)=0=\sum_nP(A_n)$. Otherwise choose $j$ with $A_j$ cocountable. For $n\ne j$, disjointness gives $A_n\subseteq\Omega\setminus A_j$, a countable set, so [F2] makes $A_n$ countable. The union is cocountable and its measure is $1=P(A_j)+\sum_{n\ne j}P(A_n)$. Also $P(\Omega)=1$ and $P$ is nonnegative, so [F3] shows that $P$ is a probability measure. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, choose]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For each $t\in U$, the singleton $\{t\}$ is in $\mathcal A$ by [F2], so $f_t=\mathbf1_{\{t\}}$ is measurable. Its integral is $Pf_t=P(\{t\})=0$. [F2, F3, given, step 2.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: For any $\omega\in\Omega$, if $\omega\in U$ then the index $t=\omega$ gives $f_t(\omega)=1$, while if $\omega\notin U$ every $t\in U$ differs from $\omega$ and all the function values are zero. Hence the displayed supremum equals $\mathbf1_U(\omega)$. Both $U$ and $\Omega\setminus U$ contain a nondegenerate interval and are uncountable by [F1]; therefore $U\notin\mathcal A$, so the supremum is nonmeasurable. [F1, step 3.1, given] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor:
For each positive integer $m$, let $N:=16^m$ be the natural number obtained by multiplying $16$ by itself $m$ times. Equip $\mathcal X_m:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with the uniform probability $Q_m(\{i\})=1/N$. For $k=0,\ldots,N$, define the threshold function $f_k:=\mathbf1_{\{1,\ldots,k\}}$, with $f_0\equiv0$. Put $\mathcal F_m:=\{f_0,\ldots,f_N\}$.

These are nested threshold indicators. Their VC-subgraph index is $V=2$, while for $r=m$ and $\epsilon=1/64$,

$$N(\epsilon,\mathcal F_m,L^m(Q_m))=N+1=16^m+1.$$

Thus a purported entropy bound whose right side has no dependence on $r$ is false even when the VC index is fixed.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: The real-power definition gives $16^1=\exp(\log16)=16$. Its exponent law gives $16^{j+1}=16^j16$ for every natural $j$, so induction identifies the real power $16^m$ with the natural product defining $N$. By [F3], $$N^{-1/m}=(16^m)^{-1/m}=16^{-1}=1/16.$$ [F3, given, algebra, induction]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: The subgraphs $C_{f_k}=\{(i,t):t<f_k(i)\}$ are nested in increasing $k$. A point $(1,1/2)$ belongs to $C_{f_N}$ and not to $C_{f_0}$, so a singleton is shattered. No two-point set is shattered by a nested family, since shattering would require both opposite singleton traces, which nested sets cannot realize. Therefore the VC-subgraph dimension is exactly one and its index is $V=2$. [F1, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For $k\ne\ell$, the functions differ on exactly $|k-\ell|$ atoms. By [F2] and [F4], $$\|f_k-f_\ell\|_{Q_m,m}=\left(\frac{|k-\ell|}{N}\right)^{1/m}\ge N^{-1/m}=1/16.$$ [F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Since $1/16>2\epsilon=1/32$, a closed $L^m(Q_m)$ ball of radius $\epsilon$ centered at a class member cannot contain two distinct class members: the triangle inequality would make their distance at most $2\epsilon$. Thus every cover needs at least $N+1$ centers; taking each member as its own center gives a cover with $N+1$. This proves the exact covering number. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: Fix any proposed right side that depends only on $\epsilon$, the VC index, and constants independent of $r$. At $\epsilon=1/64$ and $V=2$ it is a fixed finite number. By [F5], choose $m$ so large that $16^m+1$ exceeds that number. Step 3.1 then contradicts the proposed bound. The corrected bound retains $r$ in its base through $(2/\epsilon)^r$. [F5, step 3.1] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n=d\ge2$, let $1\le s\le n/2$, and take
the fixed design $X=\sqrt n\,I_n$. For
$$\Theta_s:=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^n: |\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\theta_j\ne0\}|\le s\},$$
observe $Y=X\theta+\varepsilon$ with one common noise law
$\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,\sigma^2I_n)$, where $\sigma>0$. For Borel fitted-vector
estimators $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$, define
$$R^*_{n,s}:=\inf_{T\ \mathrm{Borel}}\ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s} \mathbb E_\theta\left[\frac1n\|T(Y)-X\theta\|_2^2\right].$$
Then for $C=32(4+2\log6)$,
$$\frac{\sigma^2s\log(en/s)}{200000n} \le R^*_{n,s} \le\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s}\mathbb E_\theta\left[ \frac1n\|\widehat\mu_s(Y)-X\theta\|_2^2\right] \le C\frac{\sigma^2s\log(en/s)}n,$$
where $\widehat\mu_s$ is the constrained support-search fitted vector. Thus
this Gaussian orthogonal-sequence model has a matching minimax rate up to
universal constants. The sparse upper-bound theorem itself is choice-free; this corollary
assumes AC for its Gaussian law and Fano lower-bound suppliers.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: By [F3], the noise satisfies the centered vector proxy condition required by [F1]. The support-search fitted vector is Borel by [F2], so it is an admissible estimator for [F6]. Applying [F1] at each $\theta\in\Theta_s$ and taking the supremum and then the infimum gives the upper bound. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F6, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: Fix any Borel fitted-vector estimator $T$. Put $Z=Y/\sqrt n$ and $S(z)=T(\sqrt n z)/\sqrt n$, which is Borel by [F8]. Under the independent realization in [F4], the coordinates of $Z$ are coordinatewise measurable affine transforms of independent standard normals. By [F7], they remain independent and have laws $N(\theta_j,\sigma^2/n)$, exactly the sequence experiment in [F5]. Applying [F5] to the Borel estimator $S$ gives $$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s}\mathbb E_\theta\|S(Z)-\theta\|_2^2 \ge\frac{\sigma^2s\log(en/s)}{200000n}.$$ [A1, F4, F5, F7, F8, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Since $X=\sqrt n I_n$, pointwise $$\frac1n\|T(Y)-X\theta\|_2^2 =\left\|\frac{T(Y)}{\sqrt n}-\theta\right\|_2^2 =\|S(Z)-\theta\|_2^2.$$ By [F6] these pointwise losses define the respective risks. Thus every Borel $T$ has supremum fitted-value risk at least the lower bound in step 1.2. Taking the infimum over $T$ proves the minimax lower bound. [F6, step 1.2, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: The upper bound in step 1.1 and the lower bound in step 2.1 give the displayed comparison, with universal constants $1/200000$ and $C$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor: Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\{P_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment with nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta$. Let $\mathcal S$ be a topological space with its Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathcal S)$, and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Write $\sigma(S):=\{S^{-1}(C):C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal S)\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $S$ as in [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]]. A possibly randomized test is a measurable function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]]. For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, a **conditional rejection probability given $S$** is a supplied version $q_\theta$ of $E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$, where conditional expectation is understood as in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The test has **conditional level at most $\alpha$ given $S$ on $\Theta_0$** if such versions can be supplied with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. The almost-sure qualification is separate under each null law; no common null set or pointwise statement at conditioning values of probability zero is asserted.

read_units.claim_anchor:
A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

read_units.claim_anchor:
For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Let $(S,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. A class is **pointwise measurable** if it has a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that for each $f\in\mathcal F$ there is a sequence in $\mathcal F_0$ converging pointwise to $f$. Write $\mathbb G_n(f)=\sqrt n(P_nf-Pf)$ using [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and put

$$\rho_P(f,g)=\{P[(f-g)-P(f-g)]^2\}^{1/2}.$$

This is a pseudometric: distinct functions can have zero distance when their centered difference vanishes $P$-almost surely. The empirical process is **asymptotically equicontinuous in probability** with respect to $\rho_P$ if for every $\eta>0$,

$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^*\left(\sup_{f,g\in\mathcal F:\,\rho_P(f,g)<\delta}|\mathbb G_n(f)-\mathbb G_n(g)|>\eta\right)=0.$$

Here $P^*(A)=\inf\{P(B): A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$ is outer probability; bounded nonmeasurable functionals are handled by the corresponding outer expectation $E^*Y=\inf\{EY':Y'\text{ measurable and }Y'\ge Y\}$. For a pointwise-measurable class these conventions agree with ordinary probability whenever the displayed supremum is measurable.

Write $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ for the bounded real-valued functions on the index set $\mathcal F$, with norm $\|z\|_{\mathcal F}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z(f)|$. The class is **$P$-Donsker** if $\mathbb G_n$, as a process in this space, converges weakly in the outer-expectation sense to a tight Borel law of a centered Gaussian process $\mathbb G_P$ with covariance

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb G_P(f),\mathbb G_P(g))=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

Here outer weak convergence means $E^*H(\mathbb G_n)\to EH(\mathbb G_P)$ for every bounded uniformly continuous real function $H$ on $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$; the outer expectation is the infimum of expectations of measurable majorants. The law is tight in the sense of [[def-tight-family-of-probability-measures]]. Finite-dimensional convergence means weak convergence of the vector of process values at every finite list of indices, as in [[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]].

read_units.claim_anchor:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

read_units.claim_anchor: A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

read_units.claim_anchor:
Use the empirical-measure convention of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]: for iid observations $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ with common law $P$, $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable integrable envelope $F$, meaning $|f|\le F$ $P$-almost surely for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $PF<\infty$. It is **pointwise measurable** if there is a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence from $\mathcal F_0$. For a pointwise-measurable class, dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $Pf_k\to Pf$ along the approximating sequence, and finite empirical averages converge pointwise, so the supremum defining the uniform law is determined by $\mathcal F_0$. The class is **$P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if

$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\longrightarrow0$$

in probability. It is **strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if the same convergence holds almost surely. For an uncountable class with a countable pointwise-dense subclass, the supremum is interpreted using outer probability unless the chosen version makes it measurable. For a pointwise-measurable class the supremum is determined by the countable subclass and is measurable. That subclass has a common conull envelope bound, so the supremum is finite almost surely; after choosing a real-valued version, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability by [[thm-almost-sure-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]].

read_units.claim_anchor:
Let $M\ge2$ be an integer, let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be probability measures on
one measurable sample space, and let $J$ be uniform on $[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$.
Conditional on $J=j$, let the observation $X$ have law $P_j$. Define the
mixture law
$$\bar P:=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M P_j$$
and the **mutual information** of this finite experiment by
$$I(J;X):=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M D(P_j\|\bar P).$$
Here $D$ is the directional KL divergence of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], and logarithms are natural. Each
$P_j\ll\bar P$, since $\bar P(A)=0$ forces $P_j(A)=0$ for every $j$. Moreover,
$dP_j/d\bar P\le M$ almost everywhere, because $\bar P\ge P_j/M$ as measures;
the negative part of $t\log t$ is bounded. Thus every term in the finite sum
is well-defined and finite.

The uniform prior is part of this definition. A nonuniform prior requires its
own weights in the mixture and in the KL average.

read_units.claim_anchor:
Let $m\ge1$, let $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ be a fixed sample in a measurable space $\mathcal X$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite or countable class of measurable real functions such that the displayed supremum is finite and measurable on the finite sign space. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs. The **one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity** is

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F):=\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i f(z_i).$$

There is no absolute value in this definition and $0$ need not belong to $\mathcal F$. It differs from the absolute-value complexity $m^{-1}\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)|$.

read_units.claim_anchor:
For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a real-valued statistic whose sampling
distribution is parameter-free. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Fix one null probability law $P_0$. Let $S$ be a random element of a measurable space and let $T$ be a real random variable on the same probability space. Suppose a conditional law kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ of $T$ given $S$ is supplied, in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. On an auxiliary extension, let $U$ be independent of $(S,T)$ and have the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$, characterized by $P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$. The **randomized conditional upper-tail p-value** is
$$p_U:=K(S,(T,\infty))+U K(S,\{T\}),$$
and its **nonrandomized upper-tail value** is
$$p_0:=K(S,[T,\infty)).$$
The strict tail and atom terms are evaluated at the realized pair $(S,T)$; the independent $U$ randomizes only within the tie mass. Their measurability, including measurability of both displayed p-values, follows from [[lem-conditional-kernel-tail-and-atom-evaluations-are-measurable]]. The inclusive tail is the sum of the strict tail and the atom at $T$. This definition asserts no existence of the conditional kernel; it is supplied as part of the input.

read_units.claim_anchor:
Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ be a family of subsets of an arbitrary set $X$. For a finite $T\subseteq X$, its trace is

$$\mathcal C|_T:=\{C\cap T:C\in\mathcal C\}.$$

The family $\mathcal C$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal C|_T=\mathcal P(T)$. This extends the finite-ground-set trace convention of [[def-shattering-and-vc-dimension]]: any finite $T$ can be relabeled by $[|T|]$, and relabeling preserves all traces and their cardinalities.

For a nonempty class, its **VC dimension** $d(\mathcal C)$ is the greatest size of a finite shattered set if those sizes are bounded, is $0$ if no singleton is shattered, and is $+\infty$ if finite shattered sets have unbounded size. When the dimension is finite, its **VC index** is

$$V(\mathcal C):=d(\mathcal C)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ such that no $V$-point subset is shattered. The empty class is assigned $V=0$ by convention and is treated separately in the entropy theorem.

read_units.claim_anchor:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $\mathcal F$ be a class of measurable real-valued functions on it. The **subgraph** of $f\in\mathcal F$ is

$$C_f:=\{(x,t)\in\mathcal X\times\mathbb R:t<f(x)\}.$$

It is measurable in $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$: the coordinate lifts are measurable by [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], their difference is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and its strict negative set is measurable by [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]. The class $\mathcal F$ is a **VC-subgraph class** when the set family $\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}:=\{C_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$ has finite VC index as defined in [[def-vc-class-of-sets-and-index]]. For nonempty $\mathcal F$, write $d(\mathcal F)$ for the greatest size of a finite shattered set (zero if none is shattered) and

$$V(\mathcal F):=d(\mathcal F)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ for which no $V$-point set is shattered. If no finite such integer exists, set $V=+\infty$. The empty class is treated separately and assigned index $V=0$ by convention. Thus for every nonempty finite-index class, the VC dimension is exactly $V-1$.

A **measurable envelope** of $\mathcal F$ is a nonnegative measurable function $F$ on $\mathcal X$ such that $|f(x)|\le F(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $x\in\mathcal X$. In an $L^r(Q)$ assertion, changing $F$ on a $Q$-null set does not change its norm or the distances in that assertion.

read_units.claim_anchor: Let $G=S_3$ permute the coordinates of $\Omega=\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\subset\{0,1\}^3$, give the three points equal probability, take $T(x)=x_1$, and use an independent $U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$. Each point has a stabilizer of size two. The group-average inclusive ranks are $p_0(e_1)=1/3$ and $p_0(e_2)=p_0(e_3)=1$. The randomized values are $p_U(e_1)=U/3$ and $p_U(e_2)=p_U(e_3)=1/3+2U/3$, illustrating how tied ranks fill adjacent intervals even when each orbit point has multiple group preimages.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: The group $S_3$ permutes the three one-hot vectors transitively. Each vector has weight $1/3$, so every permutation preserves the law and the null is invariant. The permutations fixing a given coordinate position are the identity and the transposition of the other two positions; hence each orbit point is produced by exactly two of the six group elements. [F1, F4, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: At $e_1$, $T(e_1)=1$; two transformed values equal $1$ and four equal $0$. Thus $p_0(e_1)=2/6=1/3$ and $p_U(e_1)=2U/6=U/3$. At $e_2$ or $e_3$, the observed statistic is $0$; two transformed values are strictly greater and four tie, so $p_0=6/6=1$ and $p_U=(2+4U)/6=1/3+2U/3$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Under the uniform null, $e_1$ occurs with probability $1/3$, and $e_2,e_3$ together with probability $2/3$. Conditional on the first case, $p_U$ is uniform on $[0,1/3]$; conditional on the second, it is uniform on $[1/3,1]$. These intervals have lengths $1/3$ and $2/3$, equal to their mixture weights, so the mixture is uniform on $[0,1]$. The inclusive rank is $1/3$ with probability $1/3$ and $1$ with probability $2/3$, which is superuniform. [F3, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor:
Take two independent Bernoulli samples of sizes $n_1,n_2\ge1$ and test the one-sided alternative that the first success probability exceeds the second. Under the null, all $N=n_1+n_2$ trials have a common success probability $p\in[0,1]$. Let $K$ be the number of successes in the first sample and $S$ the total number in both samples. For every integer margin $s\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, define the supplied conditional-law kernel $Q$ by
$$Q(s,\{k\})=\frac{\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}}{\binom{N}{s}},\qquad \max(0,s-n_2)\le k\le\min(n_1,s),$$
and set $Q(s,\{k\})=0$ outside the displayed range. For each $s$, these weights sum to one because they count all $\binom Ns$ ways to choose the $s$ success positions according to how many lie in the first sample. At margins of positive probability this is the conditional law and it does not depend on $p$; at endpoint nulls $p=0,1$, the formula also supplies a version at the other, probability-zero margins. Large values of $K$ support the one-sided alternative that the first sample has a larger success probability. For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the conditional masses at $k=0,1,2$ are $1/6,4/6,1/6$; the inclusive upper-tail p-values are $1,5/6,1/6$.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Write $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{N}$ and give each coordinate the two-point Bernoulli$(p)$ law. By [F1], a sequence with $s$ ones has weight $p^s(1-p)^{N-s}$; the product weights sum to $(p+(1-p))^N=1$, and [F2] gives the independent-trial model. For $0<p<1$, every sequence with $S=s$ has the same positive weight. [F1, F2, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: There are $\binom{N}{s}$ sequences with $s$ successes. Exactly $\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}$ of them have $K=k$: choose $k$ of the first $n_1$ positions and $s-k$ of the other $n_2$. These counts partition all size-$s$ subsets, so the displayed kernel weights sum to one for every $s$, and when $P_p(S=s)>0$, dividing by the total count using [F3] gives the conditional mass; the feasible range is precisely where both binomial coefficients are nonzero. At $p=0$ only $S=0$ occurs and $K=0$; at $p=1$ only $S=N$ occurs and $K=n_1$, so the supplied kernel has the required conditional law on the realized margin. At the other, probability-zero margins the same formula is simply the chosen kernel extension. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the feasible values are $k=0,1,2$, with counts $1,4,1$ among the six two-success sequences. Their probabilities are therefore $1/6,4/6,1/6$. Summing the masses at or above each observed value gives inclusive p-values $1,5/6,1/6$. The strict-tail-plus-tie formulas are respectively $5/6+U/6$, $1/6+2U/3$, and $U/6$; their intervals $[5/6,1]$, $[1/6,5/6]$, and $[0,1/6]$ have lengths matching the three conditional masses. [F3, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: For each margin $s$ with $P_p(S=s)>0$, [F5] makes the nonrandomized p-value conditionally superuniform and the randomized value conditionally uniform under the null. Rejecting when the nonrandomized value is at most $\alpha$ is therefore a conditional level-$\alpha$ test, so [F6] gives unconditional size at most $\alpha$. The test function of the randomized rule is $\varphi_\alpha(x)=P_U(p_U(x,U)\le\alpha)$; it is measurable because the sample space is finite. By finite conditioning and independence of $U$, $E_p[\varphi_\alpha(X)\mid S=s]=P_p(p_U\le\alpha\mid S=s)=\alpha$, so the randomized rule has conditional and unconditional size exactly $\alpha$. At $p=0$ and $p=1$ the only observed margin has a degenerate conditional law; its inclusive value is $1$ and its randomized value is $U$, so the same validity conclusions hold. [F3, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, given] ∎

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Let $X$ be any measurable real random variable. For $a<0$, $\{e^{\lambda X}>a\}$ is the whole probability space by [F6]. For $a\ge0$ and $\lambda=0$, this set is the whole space if $a<1$ and empty if $a\ge1$. For $a\ge0$ and $\lambda\ne0$, it is the whole space when $a=0$; when $a>0$, strict increase of the exponential and the inverse relation with $\log$ give $$\{e^{\lambda X}>a\}=\begin{cases}\{X>(\log a)/\lambda\},&\lambda>0,\\\{X<(\log a)/\lambda\},&\lambda<0.\end{cases}$$ Every set on the right is measurable by [F7]. Thus $e^{\lambda X}$ is measurable by the threshold characterization, with no appeal to a continuous-map Borel measurability result qualified by Countable Choice. [F6, F7, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Put $p:=\mathbb EY$. By [F1], $p\in[0,1]$. The shifted variable $Y-p$ is measurable because $\{Y-p>a\}=\{Y>a+p\}$ for every real $a$. Applying step 1.1 to $X=Y$ and $X=Y-p$ establishes measurability of both exponentials. Applying [F2] with endpoints $0,\lambda$ gives $e^{\lambda y}\le1-y+ye^\lambda$ for every $y\in[0,1]$; taking expectations yields $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le1-p+pe^\lambda$. [F1, F2, F7, step 1.1, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Define $g(\lambda):=1-p+pe^\lambda>0$ and $\psi(\lambda):=\log g(\lambda)-p\lambda$. Positivity follows from [F6] and $p\in[0,1]$. With $q(\lambda):=pe^\lambda/g(\lambda)\in[0,1]$, [F3]–[F4] give $\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0$ and $\psi''(\lambda)=q(\lambda)(1-q(\lambda))\in[0,1/4]$. The formula also covers $p=0$ or $p=1$, since then $g$ remains positive. [given, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: The function $\psi''$ in step 3.1 is continuous. For $\lambda\ge0$, integrating twice by [F5] gives $\psi(\lambda)=\int_0^\lambda(\lambda-s)\psi''(s)\,ds\le\lambda^2/8$. For $\lambda<0$, the same endpoint formula written from $\lambda$ to $0$ gives $\psi(\lambda)=\int_\lambda^0(s-\lambda)\psi''(s)\,ds\le\lambda^2/8$. [F5, step 3.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.5.1: By step 2.1 and the exponential addition formula [F8], $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(Y-p)}=e^{-\lambda p}\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le e^{-\lambda p}g(\lambda)=e^{\psi(\lambda)}$; step 4.1 bounds this by $e^{\lambda^2/8}$. This proves the claim for every real $\lambda$, including $\lambda=0$. [F8, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

Let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Define
$$a(s,t):=K(s,(t,\infty)),\qquad b(s,t):=K(s,\{t\}).$$
Both maps are $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$-measurable. If $S_0$ and $T_0$ are measurable random elements of $S$ and $\mathbb R$ on one probability space, and $U$ is any measurable real random variable on that space, then $a(S_0,T_0)$, $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)$, and $a(S_0,T_0)+U b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable. The middle expression equals $K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Let $\pi_S:S\times\mathbb R\to S$ be the first-coordinate projection and define $\widetilde K((s,t),C):=K(s,C)$. The projection is measurable because $\pi_S^{-1}(A)=A\times\mathbb R$ for every $A\in\Sigma$; hence [F1] and [F2] show that $\widetilde K$ is a probability kernel from $(S\times\mathbb R,\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ to $\mathbb R$. [F1, F2, construct]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: The relation $\{(t,y):y>t\}$ is $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(-\infty,q)\times(q,\infty)$: density in [F3] supplies a rational strictly between $t$ and $y$, and every point in a displayed rectangle has $t<y$. The relation $\{(t,y):y<t\}$ has the analogous representation $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(q,\infty)\times(-\infty,q)$. These are countable unions of Borel rectangles by [F3] and [F4], and the equality relation is their joint complement. Therefore all three relations belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. The coordinate map $(s,t,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ is measurable because inverse images of generating rectangles are $S\times B\times C$; taking inverse images now proves the two relation indicators in the domain of $\widetilde K$ are product-measurable. [F2, F3, F4]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Apply [F5] to $\widetilde K$ and the two indicator functions of the relation sets in step 1.2. Their section integrals are $\int 1_{\{y>t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,(t,\infty))=a(s,t)$ and $\int 1_{\{y=t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,\{t\})=b(s,t)$, so both maps are product-measurable. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: The rationals are countable and dense by [F3]. For $n=2,3$, rational open boxes form a countable base of $\mathbb R^n$: each point of an open set lies in such a box contained in that set. Thus each open set is a countable union of rectangles in the finite product sigma-algebra, giving $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathbb R)^{\otimes n}$. Conversely, each coordinate projection $\pi_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, so [F7] makes $\pi_i^{-1}(A)$ Borel for every $A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$; finite intersections show every measurable rectangle is Borel, giving the reverse inclusion. Hence the Borel product and Euclidean Borel sigma-algebras agree in both dimensions. The map $\omega\mapsto(S_0(\omega),T_0(\omega))$ is measurable because the inverse image of each generating rectangle $A\times B$ is $S_0^{-1}(A)\cap T_0^{-1}(B)$; therefore $a(S_0,T_0)$ and $b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable by [F6] and [F7]. The sets $(t,\infty)$ and $\{t\}$ are disjoint and their union is $[t,\infty)$, so finite additivity gives $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)=K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$. The map $(x,z)\mapsto x+z$ is continuous by $|(x+z)-(x_0+z_0)|\le |x-x_0|+|z-z_0|$. The map $(x,z,u)\mapsto x+uz$ is continuous because $|(x+uz)-(x_0+u_0z_0)|\le |x-x_0|+|u|\cdot|z-z_0|+|z_0|\cdot|u-u_0|$, and $|u|$ is bounded in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $u_0$. The pairs and triples of the real measurable functions already obtained and $U$ are measurable because inverse images of generating product rectangles are finite intersections of coordinate preimages. The established Borel-product equalities make these continuous maps measurable by [F7]. Composition by [F7] proves measurability of the asserted sums. [F1, F2, F3, F6, F7, step 2.1] ∎

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty countable class of measurable real functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $H$, so $|g|\le H$ $P$-almost everywhere for every $g\in\mathcal G$, and $0<\|H\|_{P,2}<\infty$. Use $\mathbb G_n(g)=\sqrt n(P_ng-Pg)$ as in [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]. Suppose that for some integer $q_0\ge1$ there are nested finite partitions $\Pi_q$ of $\mathcal G$, for all $q\ge q_0$, with $m_q$ nonempty cells. For each cell $C\in\Pi_q$ choose a representative $\pi_q(C)\in C$ and define its pointwise oscillation

$$\Delta_{q,C}(x)=\sup_{g,h\in C}|g(x)-h(x)|.$$

Assume $\Delta_{q,C}$ is measurable, $0\le\Delta_{q,C}\le2H$ $P$-almost everywhere, and $\|\Delta_{q,C}\|_{P,2}\le2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}$. If $C'\in\Pi_{q+1}$ is contained in $C\in\Pi_q$, then $\Delta_{q+1,C'}\le\Delta_{q,C}$ pointwise by definition. Put

$$L_q=1+\log(2m_q),\qquad a_q=\frac{2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}}{\sqrt{L_{q+1}}},\qquad M_{\mathcal G}=\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\|g\|_{P,2}.$$

The refinement property gives $m_{q+1}\ge m_q$, so $a_q$ is nonincreasing.

There is a universal constant $C<\infty$ such that

$$\mathbb E\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|\mathbb G_n(g)|\le C\left[(M_{\mathcal G}+2^{-q_0}\|H\|_{P,2})\sqrt{L_{q_0}}+\|H\|_{P,2}\sum_{q>q_0}2^{-q}\sqrt{L_q}+\sqrt n\,P\!\left(H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}/2\}}\right)\right].$$

This is a local maximal estimate: the nested partitions and their oscillation bounds are hypotheses. Empirical-process notation uses [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]].

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: First let $h_1,\ldots,h_m$ be measurable functions with $Ph_j^2\le\sigma^2$ and $|h_j|\le b$. Applying [F2] to $h_j(X_i)-Ph_j$, whose variance is at most $\sigma^2$ and whose absolute value is at most $2b$, gives $P\{|\mathbb G_n(h_j)|>\sqrt{2\sigma^2u}+2bu/\sqrt n\}\le2e^{-u}.$ Put $L=\log(2m)$ and $Z=\max_j|\mathbb G_n(h_j)|$. By [F4], for $s\ge0$, $P\{Z>\phi(s)\}\le e^{-s},\qquad \phi(s)=\sqrt{2\sigma^2(L+s)}+2b(L+s)/\sqrt n.$ Using [F3] to integrate this tail after the increasing change of variable $t=\phi(s)$ gives $EZ\le\phi(0)+\int_0^\infty e^{-s}\phi'(s)\,ds\le C_0(\sigma\sqrt L+bL/\sqrt n)$, since $L\ge\log2$ and $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}(L+s)^{-1/2}ds\le L^{-1/2}$. The same bound follows by continuity if $\sigma=0$ or $b=0$. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: For $g\in\mathcal G$, abbreviate its cell oscillation by $\Delta_qg$. The sequence $\Delta_qg$ decreases pointwise and is dominated by $2H$, while $\|\Delta_qg\|_{P,2}\le2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}$. By [F7], $P\Delta_qg\to0$; by [F5] and the integrable majorant $2H$, the pointwise limit of $\Delta_qg$ consequently has integral zero and is zero $P$-almost everywhere. Countability of $\mathcal G$ and finiteness of each partition give one common full-measure set on which all envelope and oscillation bounds hold and every oscillation tends to zero; iid observations avoid its null complement almost surely. Define $A_qg=\prod_{p=q_0}^q\mathbf1_{\{\Delta_pg\le\sqrt n a_p\}},\quad B_{q_0}g=\mathbf1_{\{\Delta_{q_0}g>\sqrt n a_{q_0}\}},\quad B_qg=A_{q-1}g\mathbf1_{\{\Delta_qg>\sqrt n a_q\}}\ (q>q_0).$ Nestedness makes these indicators constant on the corresponding cells. At each point either every cutoff passes or there is a unique first failed cutoff. In the first case, $\pi_qg\to g$ by the vanishing oscillation; in the second, the sum stops at that first failure. In either case, pointwise telescoping gives $g-\pi_{q_0}g=(g-\pi_{q_0}g)B_{q_0}g+\sum_{q>q_0}(g-\pi_qg)B_qg+\sum_{q>q_0}(\pi_qg-\pi_{q-1}g)A_{q-1}g.$ [F4, F5, F7, given, construct, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: The $m_{q_0}$ representatives $\pi_{q_0}(C)$ have $L^2(P)$ norm at most $M_{\mathcal G}$. Clip each representative to zero on $\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}\}$. The clipped functions have absolute bound $\sqrt n a_{q_0}$ and the same $L^2$ bound, so step 1.1 bounds their expected maximum by $C_0[M_{\mathcal G}\sqrt{L_{q_0}}+a_{q_0}\log(2m_{q_0})]$. The unclipped remainders are bounded by $H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}\}}$, whose empirical-process maximum has expectation at most $2\sqrt n P(H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}\}})$. Since $m_{q_0+1}\ge m_{q_0}$, the definition of $a_{q_0}$ absorbs the second term into $2^{-q_0}\|H\|_{P,2}\sqrt{L_{q_0}}$. Thus the coarse representatives contribute at most the first and tail terms in the claimed bound, up to a universal factor. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.2: The first term on the right of step 1.2 is bounded by $2H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}/2\}}$, because $\Delta_{q_0}g>\sqrt n a_{q_0}$ and $\Delta_{q_0}g\le2H$. For any integrable $Y$, the triangle inequality and $E P_n|Y|=P|Y|$ give $E|\mathbb G_n(Y)|\le2\sqrt n P|Y|$. Thus this first term contributes at most $4\sqrt n P(H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}/2\}})$. [F1, step 1.2, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.3: Fix $q>q_0$. Because $B_qg$ is constant on its level-$q$ cell, the functions $w_q=\Delta_qg\,B_qg$ take at most $m_q$ distinct values. On $B_qg=1$, $\Delta_qg>\sqrt n a_q$ and $\Delta_qg\le\Delta_{q-1}g\le\sqrt n a_{q-1}$, so $P w_q^2\le\frac{a_{q-1}}{a_q}P(\Delta_qg)^2\le\frac{a_{q-1}}{a_q}4^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}^2,$ and $|w_q|\le\sqrt n a_{q-1}$. Step 1.1 therefore bounds the expected maximum of $|\mathbb G_n(w_q)|$ by $C_0\left[2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}\sqrt{\frac{a_{q-1}}{a_q}L_q}+a_{q-1}\log(2m_q)\right].$ For each residual $r_q=(g-\pi_qg)B_qg$, $|r_q|\le w_q$, whence $|\mathbb G_n(r_q)|\le|\mathbb G_n(w_q)|+2\sqrt n Pw_q$. The cutoff also gives $\sqrt n Pw_q\le P(\Delta_qg)^2/a_q\le2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}\sqrt{L_{q+1}}$. Since $a_{q-1}/a_q=2\sqrt{L_{q+1}/L_q}$ and $a_{q-1}=2^{-(q-1)}\|H\|_{P,2}/\sqrt{L_q}$, these bounds are at most a universal multiple of $\|H\|_{P,2}2^{-q}(\sqrt{L_q}+\sqrt{L_{q+1}})$. Summing over $q>q_0$ is bounded by a universal multiple of the entropy tail in the statement. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.4: The functions $v_q=(\pi_qg-\pi_{q-1}g)A_{q-1}g$ take at most $m_q$ distinct values by nestedness. On $A_{q-1}g=1$, both representatives lie in the level-$(q-1)$ cell, so $|v_q|\le\Delta_{q-1}g\le\sqrt n a_{q-1}$ and $Pv_q^2\le4^{-(q-1)}\|H\|_{P,2}^2$. Step 1.1 bounds their expected maximum by a universal multiple of $\|H\|_{P,2}2^{-q}\sqrt{L_q}+a_{q-1}\log(2m_q)\le C_1\|H\|_{P,2}2^{-q}\sqrt{L_q}.$ Summing over $q>q_0$ gives the same entropy-tail bound. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Apply the linear empirical-process map to the decomposition in step 1.2, then take the supremum over the countable class. Step 2.1 bounds the coarse representatives, step 2.2 bounds the first failed-cutoff term, and steps 2.3–2.4 bound the two series; the triangle inequality and [F6] justify summing their nonnegative expected maxima. Combining these estimates and increasing the universal constant gives the stated inequality. [F1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, F3, F6, algebra] ∎

Let $J\ge1$ be an integer, put $u_j=-1+2j/J$ for $j=0,\ldots,J$, and give the finite set $U_J=\{u_0,\ldots,u_J\}$ the probability weights

$$\nu_J(\{u_0\})=\nu_J(\{u_J\})=\frac1{2J},\qquad \nu_J(\{u_j\})=\frac1J\quad(1\le j<J).$$

For all $-1\le a\le b\le1$,

$$\left|\nu_J([a,b)) - \frac{b-a}{2}\right|\le\frac1J.$$

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: The weights are nonnegative and sum to $1/(2J)+(J-1)/J+1/(2J)=1$. Their finite weighted sum therefore defines a probability measure $\nu_J$ on the full power set of $U_J$; countable additivity reduces to finite additivity because $U_J$ is finite. [F1, F2, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: Define $G_J(t):=\nu_J(\{u\in U_J:u<t\})$. If $t=u_k$, the included weights have sum $0$ for $k=0$ and $(k-\tfrac12)/J$ for $1\le k\le J$, while $(t+1)/2=k/J$; the difference is at most $1/(2J)$. If $u_k<t<u_{k+1}$, then $G_J(t)=(k+\tfrac12)/J$ and $(t+1)/2\in(k/J,(k+1)/J)$, again giving difference at most $1/(2J)$. The endpoint $t=-1$ has both values zero and $t=1$ is the grid-point case $k=J$. [F2, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For $a\le b$, the grid points in $[a,b)$ are those with $u\ge a$ and $u<b$, so $\nu_J([a,b))=G_J(b)-G_J(a)$. Subtracting $(b-a)/2$ and applying step 1.2 at each endpoint gives absolute error at most $1/(2J)+1/(2J)=1/J$. [step 1.2, algebra] ∎

Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$ with $m\ge1$. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and let $U$ be independent of $J$ and uniform on $[0,1]$. Set
$$R_0:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i\ge a_J\}}{m},\qquad R_U:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i>a_J\}+U\#\{i:a_i=a_J\}}{m}.$$
Then $R_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, while $R_0$ is superuniform: $P(R_0\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Starting from the given list, repeatedly take the maximum of the remaining entries and remove every index carrying that value. By [F2] each nonempty remaining list has a maximum, and each iteration removes at least one of the original $m$ indices, so the process ends after at most $m$ iterations. It produces distinct values $b_1>b_2>\cdots>b_k$ with block sizes $r_j$. Put $c_j:=\sum_{\ell<j}r_\ell$, so $\sum_jr_j=m$. By [F1], the event that $a_J=b_j$ has probability $r_j/m$. On that event, $R_0=(c_j+r_j)/m$ and, by [A1] and [F3], $R_U=(c_j+r_jU)/m$, uniform on the interval $I_j=[c_j/m,(c_j+r_j)/m]$ of length $r_j/m$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, construct]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: The intervals $I_j$ are consecutive: the right endpoint of $I_j$ is the left endpoint of $I_{j+1}$, the first begins at $0$, and the last ends at $1$. For any Borel $B\subseteq[0,1]$, the mixture probability is $P(R_U\in B)=\sum_{j=1}^k(r_j/m)\lambda(B\cap I_j)/(r_j/m)=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda(B\cap I_j)=\lambda(B)$, since shared endpoints have Lebesgue measure zero. Thus $R_U$ is uniform. [step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For $u\in[0,1]$, $P(R_0\le u)$ is the sum of $r_j/m$ over those blocks whose right endpoint $(c_j+r_j)/m$ is at most $u$. These blocks form an initial segment; if the last is $j$, the sum telescopes to $(c_j+r_j)/m\le u$, and if there is no such block the sum is zero. Hence $P(R_0\le u)\le u$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty subset of a pseudometric space $(T,d)$, with covering and packing numbers as in [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]. For every $\epsilon>0$,

$$N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le N(\epsilon/2,\mathcal F,d).$$

The packing convention is strict separation $d(f,g)>\epsilon$; covers use closed balls of radius at most $\epsilon$ centered in $\mathcal F$.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Suppose a cover of $\mathcal F$ by $k<\infty$ closed balls of radius $\epsilon/2$ is given. Two points in the same ball have distance at most $\epsilon$ by the triangle inequality, so an $\epsilon$-separated subfamily contains at most one point from each ball. Hence every finite separated subfamily has size at most $k$, and $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le k$. Taking the least such $k$ proves $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le N(\epsilon/2,\mathcal F,d)$; if no finite cover exists the inequality is automatic. [F1, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: If $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)=+\infty$, then $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is immediate. Otherwise the finite separated cardinalities are a nonempty bounded subset of the natural numbers, so a largest size is attained by some finite separated subfamily $G\subseteq\mathcal F$. [F1, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Maximality of $G$ means each $f\in\mathcal F$ has $d(f,g)\le\epsilon$ for some $g\in G$; if all distances were greater, adding $f$ would make a larger separated subfamily. Thus the balls centered at $G$ with radius $\epsilon$ cover $\mathcal F$, so $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le|G|=D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$. [F1, step 1.2] ∎

Let $Y$ be a real random variable with cumulative distribution function $F(y)=P(Y\le y)$, and let $U$ be independent of $Y$ with the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$. Write $F(y-):=P(Y<y)$ and $\Delta F(y):=F(y)-F(y-)=P(Y=y)$. Then
$$V:=F(Y-)+U\Delta F(Y)$$
has the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$, for arbitrary continuous, discrete, mixed, or singular laws of $Y$.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: By [F1] and [F2], $F$ is nondecreasing. For each real $c$, $\{x:F(x)>c\}$ is an upper set, hence is empty, all of $\mathbb R$, or a ray with or without its finite endpoint; each such ray is Borel by [F11]. Thus every strict superlevel set is Borel, and [F10] makes $F$ Borel-measurable. For each $x$, the sets $(-\infty,x+1/n]$ decrease to $(-\infty,x]$ and have finite measure, so [F4] gives right continuity. The sets $(-\infty,-n]$ decrease to $\varnothing$ and $(-\infty,n]$ increase to $\mathbb R$, so [F3] and [F4] give the limits $0$ and $1$ at the two infinities. Also $(-\infty,x-1/n]$ increases to $(-\infty,x)$, so [F3] gives $F(x-)=\mu((-∞,x))$; [F5] then gives $F(x)-F(x-)=\mu(\{x\})$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F10, F11]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For every $x$, step 1.1 gives $F(x-)=\lim_nF(x-1/n)$. Each translate $x\mapsto F(x-1/n)$ is measurable because translation is continuous and [F8] preserves measurability under composition; [F9] makes their increasing limit $F(x-)$ measurable. Thus $\Delta F=F-F(\cdot-)$ is measurable by [F9]. Since $Y$ is measurable, $F(Y-)$ and $\Delta F(Y)$ are measurable. Because $\mathbb Q$ is countable and dense by [F12], rational open rectangles form a countable base of $\mathbb R^2$, so every Euclidean open set is a countable union of rectangles in $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. Conversely the coordinate projections are continuous, and [F8] makes the inverse image of each Borel set under either projection Borel; finite intersections then show every Borel rectangle is Euclidean Borel. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$. The pair $(U,\Delta F(Y))$ is measurable into the product sigma-algebra because preimages of generating rectangles are intersections of coordinate preimages, hence it is measurable into $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$. The map $(u,d)\mapsto ud$ is continuous, as $|ud-u_0d_0|\le |u|\cdot|d-d_0|+|d_0|\cdot|u-u_0|$ and $|u|$ is bounded near $u_0$; hence [F8] makes it Borel-measurable. Composing and then summing with $F(Y-)$ proves $V$ is measurable. [A1, F7, F8, F9, F12, step 1.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.2: Fix $0<u<1$ and set $A_u:=\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$. The upper-tail limit in step 1.1 makes $A_u$ nonempty, and the lower-tail limit makes it bounded below; hence [F6] supplies $q:=\inf A_u$. For every $n$, the infimum property gives $F(q+1/n)\ge u$, so right continuity from step 1.1 yields $F(q)\ge u$. Since $q-1/n<q$ and $q$ is a lower bound for $A_u$, $F(q-1/n)<u$; the sets $(-\infty,q-1/n]$ increase to $(-\infty,q)$, so [F3] and step 1.1 give $F(q-)=\lim_nF(q-1/n)\le u$. Put $a:=F(q-)$ and $b:=F(q)$. If $Y<q$, then $F(Y)\le a\le u$, so $V\le u$; this event has probability $a$. If $b>a$, then $P(Y=q)=b-a$ and, conditional on $Y=q$, $V=a+U(b-a)$ is uniform on $[a,b]$, contributing $(u-a)$ to $P(V\le u)$. If $b=a$, the inequalities force $a=b=u$ and $P(Y=q)=0$, so this contribution is zero. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For $Y>q$, monotonicity gives $F(Y-)\ge F(q)=b\ge u$. If $F(Y-)>u$, then $V>u$. If $F(Y-)=u$ and $\Delta F(Y)>0$, the event $V\le u$ requires $U=0$, which has probability zero by [A1]. In the remaining case $F(Y-)=F(Y)=u$, put $L:=\{y>q:F(y-)=F(y)=u\}$. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, both $F$ and $F(\cdot-)$ are Borel-measurable, so $L=\{y>q\}\cap\{F(y-)=u\}\cap\{F(y)=u\}$ is Borel and therefore $\mu$-measurable. If $L$ is empty it contributes no mass. Otherwise let $r=\sup L$, allowing $r=+\infty$ when $L$ is unbounded. For every $z$ with $q<z<r$, some $y\in L$ has $z<y$, so monotonicity gives $u=F(q)\le F(z)\le F(y-)=u$ and hence $F(z)=u$. If $r<\infty$, define $c_n=q+(r-q)n/(n+1)$; if $r=+\infty$, define $c_n=q+n$. In either case $c_n\uparrow r$ (with the limit interpreted as $+\infty$ in the second case), and [F5] gives $\mu((q,c_n])=F(c_n)-F(q)=0$. By [F3], $\mu((q,r))=0$. If finite $r$ belongs to $L$, its mass is $\Delta F(r)=0$, so $\mu(L)=0$. Thus $Y>q$ contributes no probability, and step 2.2 yields $P(V\le u)=a+(u-a)=u$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, given, construct]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: For $u_n=1/n$, the events $\{V\le u_n\}$ decrease to $\{V\le0\}$; [F4] and the formula from step 3.1 give $P(V\le0)=0$. For $v_n=1-1/n$ with $n\ge2$, the events $\{V\le v_n\}$ increase to $\{V<1\}$; [F3] and step 3.1 give $P(V<1)=1$. Finally $0\le V\le1$ by its definition, so $P(V\le1)=1$. Thus $P(V\le u)=u$ for all $u\in[0,1]$, which is the uniform law. [F3, F4, step 3.1] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor: Let $r>0$. The map $t\mapsto t^r$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$. Consequently, if $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measurable space and $h:X\to[0,\infty)$ is measurable, then $h^r$ is measurable.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: The map $t\mapsto t^r$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$. If $0<s<t$, [F1] gives positive derivative $ru^{r-1}$ at every $u\in(s,t)$, so [F4] gives $s^r<t^r$; if $s=0<t$, [F1] gives $s^r=0<t^r$. [F1, F4, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For a threshold $c<0$, $\{h^r>c\}=X$. For $c=0$, the set is $\{h>0\}$. For $c>0$, [F2] and strict increase from step 1.1 give $\{h^r>c\}=\{h>c^{1/r}\}$. Each such set is measurable because $h$ is measurable, so [F3] implies $h^r$ is measurable. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given] ∎

Let $\mathcal C$ be a nonempty class of measurable subsets of a measurable space, with finite VC index $V$ as in [[def-vc-class-of-sets-and-index]]. Let $Q$ be a probability measure, $1\le r<\infty$, and $0<\delta<1$. Put $K:=3e^2/(e-1)$. Then

$$N(\delta,\mathcal C,L^r(Q))\le\left[K\delta^{-r}\log\left(\frac{3e}{\delta^r}\right)\right]^{V-1}.$$

For sets, $\|\mathbf1_C-\mathbf1_D\|_{Q,r}=Q(C\triangle D)^{1/r}$. In the case $V=1$, the exponent is zero and the class consists of one set modulo equality, so the bound is $N=1$.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Put $d:=V-1$. If $d=0$ and two sets $C,D\in\mathcal C$ differed at a point $x$, their traces on $\{x\}$ would be both $\varnothing$ and $\{x\}$, so $\{x\}$ would be shattered, contradicting [F2]. Thus all class members are equal, $N(\delta,\mathcal C,L^r(Q))=1$, and the bound holds. [F2, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: Suppose $d\ge1$. Fix any finite subfamily $C_1,\ldots,C_m$ with pairwise $L^r(Q)$ distances greater than $\delta$, where $m\ge2$, and set $\eta:=\delta^r\in(0,1)$ and $s:=2\log(m)/\eta>0$. Let $k:=\lfloor s\rfloor$ from [F15] and $n:=k+1$; then $s<n\le s+1$. Sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ independently from $Q$ on the finite product probability space supplied by [F4]. [F1, F4, F15, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.3: For $u\ge1$, define $h(u):=u/e-\log u$. By [F10], $h'(u)=1/e-1/u$, so the mean value theorem makes $h$ decreasing on $[1,e]$ and increasing on $[e,\infty)$. Since $h(e)=0$ by [F9], $\log u\le u/e$ for every $u\ge1$. [F9, F10, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For $j\ne k$, the probability that $C_j$ and $C_k$ have identical traces on this sample is $[1-Q(C_j\triangle C_k)]^n\le(1-\eta)^n\le e^{-n\eta}$: strict separation and [F13] give $Q(C_j\triangle C_k)>\delta^r=\eta$, and then [F4] and [F6] apply. The union bound [F5] makes the probability of any collision at most $\binom m2e^{-n\eta}\le\binom m2m^{-2}<1$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, F13, step 1.2, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.2: Define $B:=K\eta^{-1}\log(3e/\eta)$. By [F9], $K=3e^2/(e-1)>e$; by [F14], $e\ge2$; also $\eta^{-1}>1$ and $\log(3e/\eta)>\log e=1$. Hence $B>e\ge2$. [F9, F14, given, algebra, step 1.2]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Consequently some sample has $m$ distinct traces on $[n]$. The induced trace family cannot shatter a set of indices containing a repeated sample value, because those two coordinates always have identical membership. Any shattered set of distinct sampled values is shattered by $\mathcal C$, so [F2] bounds its size by $d$. Applying [F3] to the induced family gives $m\le\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom nj$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, choose]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.2: If $\log m\le d$, then $m\le e^d<B^d$ by step 2.2 and monotonicity of the exponential. [F9, F11, step 2.2, algebra, step 1.2]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: If $d\ge n$, [F7], [F11], and step 2.2 give $\sum_{j=0}^d\binom nj=2^n\le2^d<B^d$, so step 3.1 gives $m<B^d$. If $d<n$, put $x:=d/n\in(0,1)$. For $j\le d$, the recursion $x^{k+1}=x^kx$ and $0<x<1$ show successively that $x^d\le x^j$. Thus [F7] and [F6] give $x^d\sum_{j=0}^d\binom nj\le\sum_{j=0}^d\binom njx^j\le(1+x)^n\le e^{nx}=e^d$, hence $\sum_{j=0}^d\binom nj\le(en/d)^d$. By step 3.1, $m\le(en/d)^d$. [F6, F7, F11, step 3.1, algebra, step 2.2]
current_proof_step_anchors.5.1: Suppose $\log m>d$. Then $n\ge2\log(m)/\eta>2d$, so $d<n$, and $\log(m)/\eta>1$ gives $n\le3\log(m)/\eta$. Combining steps 3.1 and 4.1 yields $m\le(3e\log(m)/(d\eta))^d$. Set $y:=3e/\eta$ and $z:=\exp((\log m)/d)>e$. By [F9] and [F12], $z^d=m$ and $\log z=(\log m)/d$, hence $z/\log z\le y$. [F9, F12, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra, step 1.2]
current_proof_step_anchors.6.1: In step 5.1, $z>e$ implies $u:=\log z>1$. From $z\le y\log z$, monotonicity and the product law in [F9] give $u\le\log y+\log u\le\log y+u/e$ by step 1.3. Thus $u\le\frac e{e-1}\log y$, and step 5.1 yields $z\le\frac e{e-1}y\log y=K\eta^{-1}\log(3e/\eta)=B$. Therefore $m=z^d\le B^d$ by [F11]. [F9, F11, step 5.1, step 1.3, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.7.1: If $d=0$, step 1.1 proves the result. If $d\ge1$, step 2.2 gives $B>1$, so one-member separated families satisfy the bound, and steps 4.1, 3.2, 5.1 and 6.1 bound every larger finite $\delta$-separated subfamily by $B^d$. Thus the packing number is finite and its largest integer size is attained; [F8] then gives $N(\delta,\mathcal C,L^r(Q))\le D(\delta,\mathcal C,L^r(Q))\le B^d$. Substituting $d=V-1$ proves the statement. [F8, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 4.1, step 3.2, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

Let $m\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ be fixed, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite class of real-valued functions on their domain. For each $i$, suppose $|\Phi_i(x)-\Phi_i(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, with a common $L\ge0$, and $\Phi_i(0)=0$. Then

$$\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))\right|\le2L\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i f(z_i)\right|.$$

The same holds for a countable class when the two suprema are finite for every sign vector. This is the absolute-value theorem; its factor $2$ is separate from the factor $2$ in independent-process symmetrization.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Enlarge the evaluation-vector class by adjoining the zero vector. Since $\Phi_i(0)=0$, for each sign vector both $A:=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F\cup\{0\}}\sum_i\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))$ and $B:=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F\cup\{0\}}-\sum_i\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))$ are nonnegative. The supremum of the absolute value is $\max(A,B)\le A+B$. [given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: The map $\sigma\mapsto-\sigma$ preserves the uniform sign law, so $\mathbb E_\sigma A=\mathbb E_\sigma B$. Therefore the left side is at most $2\mathbb E_\sigma A$. Applying [F1] to the enlarged class gives $\mathbb E_\sigma A\le L\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F\cup\{0\}}\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)\le L\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)|$. Combining proves the claimed factor $2L$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For a countable class, enumerate its members and apply the finite proof to increasing finite initial subclasses. For each sign vector, the finite suprema increase to the corresponding countable supremum; averaging over the finite sign cube passes the inequalities to the limit. [step 2.1, given] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor:
Under the simple null and the supplied conditional law in [[def-randomized-conditional-p-value]], for every $u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_0(p_U\le u\mid\sigma(S))=u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely},$$
while the nonrandomized upper-tail value satisfies
$$P_0(p_0\le u\mid\sigma(S))\le u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely}.$$
Thus the randomized value is conditionally uniform and the inclusive-tail value is conditionally superuniform, including when the conditional law has atoms.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: For each $s$, let $\Lambda_s:=K(s,\cdot)\otimes\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the uniform law of $U$. By [F4] this is a probability measure with rectangle values $\Lambda_s(C\times D)=K(s,C)\lambda(D)$. For $A\in\sigma(S)$ and Borel $C,D$, the conditional-law identity [F2] gives $\int_A\Lambda_S(C\times D)\,dP_0=\lambda(D)P_0(A\cap\{T\in C\})$. Independence in [F3] makes the right side $P_0(A\cap\{T\in C,U\in D\})$. The class of product-Borel sets where the evaluation $s\mapsto\Lambda_s(E)$ is measurable and every such conditional identity holds is a Dynkin system: complements subtract from the probability-one whole-space evaluation, and disjoint unions follow by countable additivity and increasing limits. It contains the generating rectangles, so [F5] and [F6] extend measurability and the conditional identity to every product-Borel set. Thus $\Lambda_S$ is a conditional law of $(T,U)$ given $S$. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, A1]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For almost every conditioning value $s$, the conditional law just constructed makes $T$ have law $K(s,\cdot)$ and keeps $U$ independent uniform. Write $F_s(t):=K(s,(-\infty,t])$ and $\Delta_s(t):=F_s(t)-F_s(t-)$. By [F7], $V=F_s(T-)+(1-U)\Delta_s(T)$ is uniform, since $1-U$ is also uniform. The p-value formula in [F1] gives $p_U=1-V$, so $p_U$ is conditionally uniform. [A1, F1, F7, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For the same $s$, $p_0=1-F_s(T-)$ and $p_U=1-F_s(T-)-(1-U)\Delta_s(T)\le p_0$. Hence $\{p_0\le u\}\subseteq\{p_U\le u\}$ conditionally on $S=s$. Step 2.1 gives $P_0(p_0\le u\mid S=s)\le u$. This holds for each $u\in[0,1]$ and almost every conditioning value, proving conditional superuniformity. [F1, step 2.1, A1, algebra] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor: Let $\varphi$ be a test for nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]], let $S$ be a statistic, and let $\alpha\in[0,1]$. If for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$ there is a conditional-expectation version $q_\theta=E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$ with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely, then $E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\le\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. Consequently, the test has size at most $\alpha$, where size is the supremum of its rejection expectation over the null family as in [[def-test-size-and-power]].

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Fix $\theta\in\Theta_0$ and choose the conditional version $q_\theta$ supplied by [F1]. Taking $A=\Omega$ in [F2] gives $E_\theta q_\theta=E_\theta\varphi(X)$. [F1, F2, given, choose]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Since $q_\theta\le\alpha$ almost surely and both variables are integrable, [F3] gives $E_\theta q_\theta\le E_\theta\alpha=\alpha$. Combining with step 1.1 yields $E_\theta\varphi(X)\le\alpha$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: The argument holds for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$, so taking the supremum of these rejection expectations gives size at most $\alpha$ under the convention [A1]. No common exceptional null set across parameter values is needed. [A1, step 2.1] ∎

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal S,\mathscr S)$ be standard Borel spaces as in [[def-standard-borel-space]]. Fix Polish topologies realizing these specified Borel sigma-algebras, as the standard-Borel definition permits. Let $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint parameter subsets, and write $\{P_\eta:\eta\in\Theta_0\}$ for the null subfamily. Let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Suppose there is one probability kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ such that, for every $\eta\in\Theta_0$, $K(S,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full data $X$ given $\sigma(S)$ under $P_\eta$. This is the common-kernel premise of sufficiency for the null subfamily in [[def-sufficient-statistic]]. For any measurable $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, define
$$q(s):=\int_{\mathcal X}\varphi(x)K(s,dx).$$
Then $q$ is measurable and $q(S)$ is a version of the conditional rejection probability of $\varphi$ given $S$ under every $P_\eta$. The same function $q$ works for every nuisance value, with conditional-expectation identities interpreted almost surely under each corresponding law.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: The map $(s,x)\mapsto\varphi(x)$ is product-measurable by [F5]. Kernel integration [F2] therefore makes $q$ measurable. Since $K(s,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $0\le\varphi\le1$, every value satisfies $0\le q(s)\le1$. [F2, F5, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Fix $\eta\in\Theta_0$. By [A1] and [F1], $K(S,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(S)$ under $P_\eta$. Applying [F3] to the bounded function $\varphi$ shows that for every $A\in\sigma(S)$, $\int_A q(S)\,dP_\eta=\int_A\varphi(X)\,dP_\eta$. Thus $q(S)$ is a version of the conditional rejection probability under this null law. The same kernel in [A1] defines the same $q$ for every $\eta$, proving nuisance-freeness; only the individual laws' almost-sure qualifications are used. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor:
Let $(T,d)$ be a nonempty pseudometric space that is totally bounded in the following sense: for every $r>0$ there is a finite set $E_r\subseteq T$ such that $T\subseteq\bigcup_{e\in E_r}\{t\in T:d(t,e)\le r\}$. Its diameter is $D:=\sup_{s,t\in T}d(s,t)<\infty$. For each $t\in T$, let $X_t$ be a real random variable. Assume the process is separable: a specified countable dense subset $T_0\subseteq T$, equipped with a fixed listing, has the property that the supremum of every process increment over $T$ equals its supremum over $T_0$ almost surely. Suppose all increments are centered and sub-Gaussian with their $d$-scale, meaning that for every $s,t\in T$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(X_s-X_t)\}\le\exp\{\lambda^2d(s,t)^2/2\}.$$

If

$$\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N(\epsilon,T,d)$ is the least number of closed $d$-balls of radius $\epsilon$ covering $T$ ([[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]), then for every $t_0\in T$,

$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\le C\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon$$

for a universal constant $C$. If $D=0$, the integral and the supremum are both zero.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: First derive a finite-maximum estimate. If $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ are centered and each has sub-Gaussian proxy at most $s^2$, then for $\lambda>0$, $\mathbb E e^{\lambda\max_j|Y_j|}\le\sum_{j=1}^m(\mathbb Ee^{\lambda Y_j}+\mathbb Ee^{-\lambda Y_j})\le2m e^{\lambda^2s^2/2}.$ By [F3], $\mathbb E\max_j|Y_j|\le\lambda^{-1}\log(2m)+\lambda s^2/2$. For $s>0$, choosing $\lambda=\sqrt{2\log(2m)}/s$ gives $\mathbb E\max_j|Y_j|\le s\sqrt{2\log(2m)}$; for $s=0$, the proxy bound forces every $Y_j=0$ almost surely by [F4] applied to $e^{\pm\lambda Y_j}$ and letting $\lambda\to\infty$. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: If $D=0$, every pair in $T$ has distance zero. The proxy-zero case of step 1.1 applied to each increment, together with separability and [F6] for the countable intersection of probability-one events, makes the supremum zero. Assume $D>0$. Fix $k\ge1$ and put $\epsilon_k=2^{-k}D$. Total boundedness gives a finite cover of $T$ by $N(\epsilon_k/4,T,d)$ closed balls of radius $\epsilon_k/4$. Approximate each center by a point of the dense set $T_0$ within $\epsilon_k/4$ to obtain a cover of $T$ by the same number of balls of radius $\epsilon_k/2$. Since the specified countable dense set is listed, choose the first finite tuple under its induced enumeration that is an $\epsilon_k$-net and has cardinality at most this cover size; such a tuple exists by the construction. Denote it by $T_k$. For each $t$, choose the least-index point $\pi_k(t)\in T_k$ within $\epsilon_k$. These canonical choices across scales require no choice axiom. Put $T_0^{(0)}=\{t_0\}$ and $\pi_0(t)=t_0$. [F1, F6, step 1.1, given, construct]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.2: For a finite subset $A\subset T_0$, telescope $X_t-X_{t_0}$ through $\pi_1(t),\ldots,\pi_m(t)$ for every $t\in A$. At level $1$ there are at most $|T_1|$ increments, each with proxy at most $D^2$; for $k\ge2$ there are at most $|T_k||T_{k-1}|$ increments, each with proxy at most $(\epsilon_k+\epsilon_{k-1})^2=(3\epsilon_k)^2$. Applying step 1.1 to the finite set of increments at each level, and the triangle inequality for their maxima, yields $\mathbb E\max_{t\in A}|X_{\pi_m(t)}-X_{t_0}|\le C_1\sum_{k=1}^m\epsilon_k\sqrt{1+\log N(\epsilon_k/4,T,d)}$ for a universal $C_1$; the $k=1$ term is absorbed using $\epsilon_1=D/2$ and $N(\epsilon_1/4)\ge1$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: The residual maximum over $A$ has expectation at most $\epsilon_m\sqrt{2\log(2|A|)}$ by step 1.1, since $d(t,\pi_m(t))\le\epsilon_m$. Letting $m\to\infty$ for this fixed finite $A$ removes the residual. The dyadic sum in step 2.2 is bounded by a universal multiple of the entropy integral: on each interval $[\epsilon_k/8,\epsilon_k/4]$, monotonicity of $N$ makes the integral at least $(\epsilon_k/8)\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon_k/4,T,d)}$. Also, for $0<\epsilon<D/2$, one ball of radius $\epsilon$ cannot cover a set of diameter $D$, so $N(\epsilon,T,d)\ge2$ and the entropy integral is at least $(D/2)\sqrt{\log2}$; this absorbs the geometric contribution from the added $1$. Hence $\mathbb E\max_{t\in A}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\le C\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon.$ Taking an increasing sequence of finite subsets whose union is $T_0$, [F5] and the separability assumption give the asserted supremum over $T$. [F1, F5, step 2.2, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

Let $M\ge2$ be finite, let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be sample laws on one
measurable space, and let $t_1,\ldots,t_M$ lie in a metric space
$(\mathcal T,\rho)$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Suppose
$\rho(t_j,t_l)\ge\Delta>0$ whenever $j\ne l$. Let $J$ be uniform on
$[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$, with conditional observation law $P_j$ given $J=j$.
For any probability reference law $Q$, define
$$K_Q:=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M D(P_j\|Q)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For every randomized estimator kernel from the observation to $\mathcal T$,
with squared metric loss $\rho(a,t_j)^2$, its uniform average risk and its
maximum risk are each at least
$$\frac{\Delta^2}{4} \left(1-\frac{K_Q+\log2}{\log M}\right).$$
The minimax risk over all randomized estimators obeys this bound as well.
When $K_Q=+\infty$, the displayed lower bound is interpreted as $-\infty$
and is vacuous. Logarithms are natural.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Since $\bar P\ge P_j/M$, each $P_j\ll\bar P$. Choose densities $p_j=dP_j/d\bar P$ and set $\pi_j=p_j/M$. Then $\sum_j\pi_j=1$ $\bar P$-almost everywhere and $0\le\pi_j\le1$. The mutual-information definition [F1] and KL formula [F2] give $I(J;X)=\int\sum_j\pi_j\log(M\pi_j)\,d\bar P=\log M-\int H(\pi(x))\,\bar P(dx).$ All terms are integrable because $u\log u$ is bounded on $[0,1]$ and the sum is finite. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Let $L$ be any randomized decision in $[M]$ based on $X$, with $q_l(x)=P(L=l\mid X=x)$ given by its probability kernel. Put $w_l=\int q_l\,d\bar P$. When $w_l>0$, the conditional probability vector of $J$ given $L=l$ has entries $\eta_{lj}=w_l^{-1}\int q_l(x)\pi_j(x)\,\bar P(dx)$. Apply Jensen to $u\mapsto u\log u$ for each coordinate under the probability measure $q_l\,d\bar P/w_l$, sum over $j$, and use $\sum_j\pi_j=\sum_j\eta_{lj}=1$. The result is $H(\eta_l)\ge w_l^{-1}\int q_l(x)H(\pi(x))\,\bar P(dx)$. Multiplication by $w_l$ and summation over positive $w_l$ yields $H(J\mid L):=\sum_lw_lH(\eta_l)\ge\int H(\pi(x))\,d\bar P$; zero-probability outputs contribute zero. Hence $\log M-H(J\mid L)\le I(J;X)$ by step 1.1. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.2: If some $P_j\not\ll Q$, then $K_Q=+\infty$ and the bound is vacuous. Otherwise write $r_j=dP_j/dQ$. If the positive part of $r_j\log r_j$ has infinite integral, then $D(P_j\|Q)=+\infty$; if it is finite, the negative part is finite by [F2] and Jensen [F3] for the convex function $u\log u$ gives $D(P_j\|Q)=\int r_j\log r_j\,dQ\ge0$. Thus every divergence is nonnegative; therefore $K_Q<\infty$ implies that every term is finite. Set $\bar r=M^{-1}\sum_jr_j=d\bar P/dQ$. On $\{\bar r>0\}$, $r_j=M\bar r\pi_j$ $Q$-almost everywhere: by [F2], for every measurable $A$, $P_j(A)=\int_Ap_j\,d\bar P=\int_Ap_j\bar r\,dQ$, where $p_j=dP_j/d\bar P=M\pi_j$ from step 1.1; uniqueness of the density gives the identity. Hence $r_j\log(r_j/\bar r)=M\bar r\,\pi_j\log(M\pi_j)$, whose positive and negative parts are integrable because $0\le\pi_j\le1$, $u\log u$ is bounded on $[0,1]$, and $\bar r$ has integral one. The identity $r_j\log r_j=r_j\log(r_j/\bar r)+r_j\log\bar r$ holds there; on $\{\bar r=0\}$ all $r_j=0$ and every term is set to zero. Jensen and [F3] give $\bar r\log\bar r\le M^{-1}\sum_jr_j\log r_j$, so its positive part is integrable; its negative part is bounded by [F2]. Integrating the identity and averaging therefore gives $K_Q=I(J;X)+D(\bar P\|Q).$ Finally Jensen under the probability law $Q$ yields $D(\bar P\|Q)=\int\bar r\log\bar r\,dQ\ge(\int\bar r\,dQ)\log(\int\bar r\,dQ)=0$. Therefore $I(J;X)\le K_Q$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For the error event $E=\{L\ne J\}$, $E$ is determined by $(J,L)$, so $H(E,J\mid L)=H(J\mid L)$. Expanding the finite conditional entropy sums and factoring $P(E=e,J=j\mid L=l)=P(E=e\mid L=l)P(J=j\mid E=e,L=l)$ gives $H(J\mid L)=H(E\mid L)+H(J\mid E,L).$ For each conditional law, entropy on at most $N$ points is at most $\log N$: if its probabilities are $s_1,\ldots,s_N$, Jensen for $u\log u$ gives $N^{-1}\sum_r(Ns_r)\log(Ns_r)\ge0$, which rearranges to $-\sum_rs_r\log s_r\le\log N$. Thus $H(E\mid L)\le\log2$; when $E=0$, $J=L$ has entropy zero, and when $E=1$, at most $M-1$ indices remain, so $H(J\mid E,L)\le P(E=1)\log(M-1)\le P(E=1)\log M$. Combining this with step 2.1 and $I(J;X)\le K_Q$ from step 2.2 proves $P(L\ne J)\ge1-\frac{K_Q+\log2}{\log M}$ when $K_Q<\infty$; for $K_Q=\infty$ the bound is vacuous. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: Given an estimator action $A\in\mathcal T$, choose $L$ to be the smallest index minimizing $\rho(A,t_l)$. This is a measurable finite-valued decision because each distance to a fixed target is continuous and ties are resolved by the fixed index order; composing the map with the estimator kernel gives the randomized decision kernel of step 2.1 by [F5]. If $L\ne J=j$, nearest choice and the triangle inequality give $\Delta\le\rho(t_j,t_L)\le\rho(t_j,A)+\rho(A,t_L)\le2\rho(A,t_j)$, so squared loss is at least $\Delta^2/4$ on the error event. Step 3.1 therefore gives the average risk bound. The maximum risk is at least its uniform average; taking the infimum over procedures using [F6] and [F7] gives the minimax conclusion. [F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
