Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID observations with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable functions $f:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. For every $\epsilon>0$,

$$P\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\ge\epsilon\right)\le2|\mathcal F|e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.$$

Here $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(Z_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. The proof uses only scalar exponential moments and finite independence; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Fix $f\in\mathcal F$ and put $Y_i=f(Z_i)$. By [F2]–[F3], the $Y_i$ are measurable independent real random variables. By [F4], $\mathbb E Y_i=Pf$. The translation in [F9] is Borel measurable, so applying [F3] to $W_i:=Y_i-Pf$ shows that the $W_i$ are measurable, independent, and centered. Also $0\le Y_i\le1$ almost surely. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F9, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, apply [F5] to $Y_i$, whose range is $[0,1]$, to obtain $\mathbb E e^{\lambda W_i}=\mathbb E e^{\lambda(Y_i-\mathbb E Y_i)}\le e^{\lambda^2/8}$. By [F9], $t\mapsto e^{\lambda t}$ is Borel measurable, so applying [F3] to the independent $W_i$ shows that $e^{\lambda W_i}$ are measurable and independent. Their expectations are finite by the displayed bound. The exponential addition formula and the nonnegative product case of [F6] now give $$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\sum_i W_i}=\mathbb E\prod_i e^{\lambda W_i}=\prod_i\mathbb E e^{\lambda W_i}\le e^{n\lambda^2/8}.$$ The sum in the left exponential is measurable by [F9]'s arithmetic-measurability clause and composition clause. [F5, F6, F9, step 1.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For $\lambda>0$, [F7] and step 2.1 give $P(\sum_i W_i\ge n\epsilon)\le\exp(-\lambda n\epsilon+n\lambda^2/8)$. Setting $\lambda=4\epsilon$ gives $P(P_nf-Pf\ge\epsilon)\le e^{-2n\epsilon^2}$. [F1, F7, step 2.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: Applying step 3.1's Markov argument to $-\sum_iW_i$ uses the bound from step 2.1 at $\lambda=-4\epsilon$ (obtained by applying [F5] to each $Y_i$) and gives $P(P_nf-Pf\le-\epsilon)\le e^{-2n\epsilon^2}$. The finite union bound [F8] therefore gives $P(|P_nf-Pf|\ge\epsilon)\le2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}$. [F1, F5, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.5.1: The event in the statement is the union over the finite class of the events in step 4.1. A second application of [F8] gives the stated factor $2|\mathcal F|$. [F8, step 4.1] ∎

read_units.claim_anchor: In a finite-group randomization setup, fix a null law invariant under the group action. Conditional on every orbit $O$ with positive probability, the data are uniform on the distinct points of $O$. For the orbit ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]], the inclusive p-value $p_0$ is superuniform under the null, and the independent-uniform tie-randomized value $p_U$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on each positive-probability orbit. Consequently, $p_U$ is also Uniform$(0,1)$ unconditionally.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Fix a positive-probability orbit $O$ and points $x,y\in O$. Choose $h\in G$ with $y=h\cdot x$. Invariance gives $P(X=y)=P(h\cdot X=y)=P(X=h^{-1}\cdot y)=P(X=x)$. Thus all $|O|$ distinct points have equal mass; by [F3] their conditional probabilities given $X\in O$ are each $1/|O|$. [A1, F1, F3, given, choose, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For fixed $x\in O$, define its stabilizer $G_x:=\{g\in G:g\cdot x=x\}$. If $y=h\cdot x$, then $\{g:g\cdot x=y\}=hG_x$: every $hg$ with $g\in G_x$ sends $x$ to $y$, and if $g\cdot x=y$ then $h^{-1}g\in G_x$. Hence every distinct point of $O$ occurs exactly $|G_x|$ times in the group-transformed list. The strict and tied counts and denominator in [F2] all have this same factor, so the group-average ranks equal the ranks computed on the distinct orbit points. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Conditional on $O$, [step 1.1] makes the observed orbit point a uniform index in the finite list $(T(y))_{y\in O}$. By [F5] and [A2], the randomizer remains independent and uniform. Apply [F4] to this list and use [step 2.1]: $p_U$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ and $P(p_0\le u\mid X\in O)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$. [F2, F4, F5, A2, step 1.1, step 2.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: The positive-probability orbits form a finite partition up to null orbits. Summing the conditional superuniform bounds from step 3.1 with weights $P(X\in O)$ gives $P(p_0\le u)\le u$; summing the conditional uniform laws gives $p_U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n>p\ge1$ whose $p$ columns are linearly independent. Use the experiment on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ indexed by $(\beta,\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^p\times(0,\infty)$, with observation $Y=X\beta+\varepsilon$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Define the least-squares statistic and residual sum of squares by
$$\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY,\qquad P_X=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad RSS_X=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad S^2=\frac{RSS_X}{n-p},\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
For every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$\widetilde T_c:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{S\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-p},\qquad \frac{RSS_X}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-p}^2,$$
and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$, with $S>0$ almost surely.

For nested deterministic full and reduced design spaces $W_R\subset W_U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of dimensions $p-q$ and $p$, where $q$ is an integer and $1\le q\le p<n$, let $P_R,P_U$ be the orthogonal projections onto these spaces and define $RSS_R=\|(I-P_R)Y\|^2$ and $RSS_U=\|(I-P_U)Y\|^2$. Under the null hypothesis that the mean vector belongs to $W_R$,
$$\widetilde F:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q}{RSS_U/(n-p)},&RSS_U>0,\\ 0,&RSS_U=0 \end{cases} \sim F_{q,n-p}.$$
The numerator and denominator chi-square contributions are independent. All t and F denominator degrees of freedom in the statement are positive.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: By full column rank, the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. Apply [F2] to obtain orthonormal columns of $Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with the same successive spans. Expressing each column of $X$ in this basis gives $X=QR$, where $R$ is upper triangular; its diagonal entries are the nonzero Gram–Schmidt residual norms, so $R$ is invertible. By [F3], extend the columns of $Q$ to an orthonormal basis $[Q\ Q_0]$ of $\mathbb R^n$. [F2, F3, choose]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Set $U=[Q\ Q_0]$. Then $U$ is orthogonal. Standardizing the independent errors gives $\eta=\varepsilon/\sigma$ with independent standard-normal coordinates, so [F4] makes $U^T\eta=(Z_Q,Z_0)$ a standard-normal product vector with independent coordinate blocks. Since $X=QR$ and $X^TX=R^TR$, the normal-equation solution in [F1] is $\widehat\beta=R^{-1}Q^TY=\beta+\sigma R^{-1}Z_Q$. Substituting $X=QR$ and $(R^TR)^{-1}=R^{-1}R^{-T}$ gives $P_X=Q R(R^TR)^{-1}R^TQ^T=Q[RR^{-1}R^{-T}R^T]Q^T=QQ^T$, because $RR^{-1}=I_p$ and $R^{-T}R^T=I_p$. Since $U$ is orthogonal, $I_n-P_X=Q_0Q_0^T$. Thus $(I_n-P_X)Y=\sigma Q_0Z_0$, so $RSS_X/\sigma^2=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$ by [F5]. By [A2] and [F7], the linear maps defining $\widehat\beta$ and $Q_0Z_0$, and the squared-norm map defining $RSS_X$, are Borel; hence these quantities are measurable functions of the independent coordinate blocks and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$ by [F4]. The map defining $\widehat\beta$ is linear and Borel, so it is a statistic for the stated experiment. The residual map and squared norm are continuous, so $RSS_X$ and $S$ are continuous. The piecewise t version in the Statement is Borel: its quotient is continuous on the Borel set $S>0$ and its value on $S=0$ is constant. Its denominator has positive degree $n-p$, hence $S>0$ almost surely by [F5]. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For $c\ne0$, put $v=R^{-T}c$. Invertibility of $R$ gives $v\ne0$. Complete $v/\|v\|$ to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^p$ by [F3]; applying [F4] to the resulting orthogonal matrix shows $G_c=v^TZ_Q/\|v\|\sim N(0,1)$. Under [A2], the continuous linear map defining $G_c$ is Borel. It is independent of $Q_0:=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$, because $Z_Q$ and $Z_0$ are independent blocks and $G_c$ and the squared-norm map are measurable functions of those blocks. Since $X^TX=R^TR$, $\|v\|^2=c^TR^{-1}R^{-T}c=c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c$. Thus on $Q_0>0$ the displayed contrast ratio is $G_c/\sqrt{Q_0/(n-p)}$; on $Q_0=0$ its version $\widetilde T_c$ is zero. This is exactly the extension in the definition of $t_{n-p}$, so [F5]–[F6] give $\widetilde T_c\sim t_{n-p}$. [A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: For the nested models, let $W_D=W_U\cap W_R^\perp$. The finite-dimensional orthogonal decompositions in [F3] give $\mathbb R^n=W_R\oplus W_D\oplus W_U^\perp$, with dimensions $p-q,q,n-p$. Choose orthonormal bases in these three spaces and concatenate them into an orthogonal matrix $V$. By [F4], the coordinates of $V^T\varepsilon/\sigma$ in the three blocks are independent standard normals. Under the null, $P_R(X\beta)=P_U(X\beta)=X\beta$, so $(I-P_R)Y=(I-P_R)\varepsilon=P_{W_D}\varepsilon+P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$ and $(I-P_U)Y=(I-P_U)\varepsilon=P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$: here [F8] identifies $I-P_R=P_{W_R^\perp}$ and $I-P_U=P_{W_U^\perp}$, while the direct sum in [F3] splits the first projection into the two orthogonal components. The coordinate-block maps and the linear projections are continuous, and squared norms are continuous, so [A2] and [F7] make all these random vectors and real variables measurable. Orthogonality and [F9] give $RSS_R-RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{q}G_j^2$ and $RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2$, where the $G$ and $H$ coordinate blocks are independent standard-normal blocks. By [F5] these sums are independent $\sigma^2\chi_q^2$ and $\sigma^2\chi_{n-p}^2$ variables; both degrees are positive. The piecewise ratio $\widetilde F$ is Borel, since it is continuous on the Borel set $RSS_U>0$ and constant on $RSS_U=0$. Its value is the scaled ratio on $Q_H:=\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2>0$ and $0$ when $Q_H=0$; by [F6] this is exactly the defined $F_{q,n-p}$ version. The F denominator is positive almost surely by [F5], so $\widetilde F\sim F_{q,n-p}$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,d\ge1$, $\sigma>0$, and let
$1\le s\le d/2$ be integers. Observe $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ with independent
coordinates $Z_j\sim N(\theta_j,\sigma^2/n)$ for a parameter
$$\Theta_{s,d}:=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d: |\{j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}:\theta_j\ne0\}|\le s\}.$$
For every Borel estimator $T:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$,
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{s,d}} \mathbb E_\theta\|T(Z)-\theta\|_2^2 \ge \frac{\sigma^2s\log(ed/s)}{200000n}.$$

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Choose the code $\mathcal C$ from [F1], with cardinality $M$. Since $ed/s\ge2e>1$ by [F9], [F8] gives $\log(ed/s)>0$; hence $M\ge2$. Put $$a:=\sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2\log M}{4ns}}>0,\qquad \theta^\omega=a u^\omega \quad(\omega\in\mathcal C).$$ Every $\theta^\omega$ belongs to $\Theta_{s,d}$, and distinct code targets have squared distance greater than $a^2s/2$. [F1, F8, F9, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: Now suppose $M=2$. By [F8], $\log2=\int_1^2dt/t\le1$, because $1/t\le1$ on $[1,2]$. Hence [F1] gives $s\log(ed/s)\le1024$. Consider the two parameters $0$ and $b e_1$, where $b=\sigma/(2\sqrt n)$; both belong to $\Theta_{s,d}$. By [F2], their sequence laws have KL divergence $nb^2/(2\sigma^2)=1/8$, so [F4] gives total variation at most $1/4$. For the Borel vector estimator $T$, its first coordinate $T_1$ is Borel, and [F7] makes it an admissible scalar kernel. Pointwise, $$\|T(z)-\theta\|_2^2\ge|T_1(z)-\theta_1|^2$$ for both parameters. Applying [F5] to this scalar kernel shows the maximum vector risk is at least $$\frac{b^2}{8}\left(1-\frac14\right) =\frac{3\sigma^2}{128n} >\frac{1024\sigma^2}{200000n} \ge\frac{\sigma^2s\log(ed/s)}{200000n}.$$ [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F7, F8, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Take the reference law $Q=P_0$ of the zero-mean sequence. By [F2], $$D(P_{\theta^\omega}\|P_0) =\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}\|a u^\omega\|_2^2 =\frac{na^2s}{2\sigma^2}=\frac{\log M}{8}$$ for every $\omega$, since $u^\omega$ has exactly $s$ ones. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: First suppose $M\ge3$. Since $3>2\sqrt2$ (squaring gives $9>8$), [F8] implies $\log3>\log(2\sqrt2)=\frac32\log2$. Thus $\log2/\log M<2/3$. The average reference KL ratio in [F3] is $1/8$ by step 2.1, so the Fano factor is greater than $1-1/8-2/3=5/24>1/5$. With separation $\Delta=a\sqrt{s/2}$, [F3] gives uniform average risk greater than $$\frac{\Delta^2}{20}=\frac{a^2s}{40} =\frac{\sigma^2\log M}{160n} \ge\frac{\sigma^2s\log(ed/s)}{163840n} >\frac{\sigma^2s\log(ed/s)}{200000n}.$$ The maximum risk dominates this finite-code average; the Borel estimator is an admissible kernel by [F7]. Thus its supremum risk satisfies the same lower bound. [A1, F3, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: The cases $M\ge3$ and $M=2$ exhaust the possibilities by step 1.1. Step 3.1 proves the $M\ge3$ case, and step 1.2 proves the $M=2$ case. Thus the claimed lower bound holds for the arbitrary Borel estimator $T$, with risk understood as in [F6]. [F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎

Let $\mathcal X=\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $\mathsf P$ be a parametric statistical experiment on $\mathcal X$. Define the mean estimand by $\mu(\theta)=\int x\,P_\theta(dx)$ and suppose it is finite for every $\theta$. For a fixed $\theta$, suppose an IID sequence $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ with one-observation law $P_\theta$ is given and $\mathbb E_\theta|X_1|<\infty$. The sample-mean estimator $T_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ is consistent in probability for $\mu$ at $\theta$ in the IID sample-size experiments.

The assertion is pointwise in $\theta$. The existence of a common probability space carrying the IID sequence is part of the hypothesis.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: The statistical experiment and parametric model in [F11]–[F12] specify the sampling law $P_\theta$. The map $T_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ is measurable by [F9] into the Borel target [F13], so it is the estimator in [F5]; applied to the given sequence, it is the finite sample mean in [F2]. By [F1] and [F3], the law of $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$. Since $X_1$ has law $P_\theta$ and is integrable, [F10] gives $\mathbb E_\theta X_1=\int x\,P_\theta(dx)=\mu(\theta)$; the mean is the estimand [F7]. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: The hypotheses of [F4] hold for this IID sequence, so $\overline X_n\to\mathbb E_\theta X_1=\mu(\theta)$ in probability on its given common probability space. [F1, F4, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: For each $n$, step 1.1 identifies the joint data law with $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$; applying the same measurable sample-mean map therefore gives exactly the error probabilities in [F6] for the absolute-value metric [F14]. Step 1.2 makes those probabilities tend to zero for every $\varepsilon>0$, which is consistency at $\theta$. No infinite-product extension is constructed or needed. [F5, F6, F14, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID observations with law $P$, and let $Z_1',\ldots,Z_n'$ be an independent IID copy. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent uniform signs, independent of both samples. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty countable class of measurable $P$-integrable real functions. Assume the two suprema below are finite almost surely. If $\Phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is finite, convex, and nondecreasing, then

$$\mathbb E\Phi\!\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(f(Z_i)-Pf)\right|\right)\le \mathbb E\Phi\!\left(2\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i)\right|\right).$$

The same statement holds for an uncountable class when a specified countable subclass gives the same three displayed suprema almost surely for the data, copy, and signs. This is an expectation inequality only; a tail form requires separate assumptions.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: First let $\mathcal F_0\subset\mathcal F$ be finite. For fixed observed values $z_1,\ldots,z_n$, write $D_f:=\sum_i(f(z_i)-f(Z_i'))$. Then $\sum_i(f(z_i)-Pf)=\mathbb E_{Z'}D_f$. For each $f$, $|\mathbb E_{Z'}D_f|\le\mathbb E_{Z'}|D_f|\le\mathbb E_{Z'}\max_{g\in\mathcal F_0}|D_g|$; taking the finite maximum and applying monotonicity of $\Phi$ and Jensen [F3] gives $\Phi(\max_f|\sum_i(f(z_i)-Pf)|)\le\mathbb E_{Z'}\Phi(\max_f|D_f|)$. Integrating over the observations and using [F4] proves $\mathbb E\Phi(\max_f|\sum_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)|)\le\mathbb E_{Z,Z'}\Phi(\max_f|\sum_i(f(Z_i)-f(Z_i'))|)$. [F1, F3, F4, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: By [F6], each $Z_i$ and $Z_i'$ has law $P$; by [F2] and the independent-copy hypothesis, all $2n$ coordinates have product law. [F7] makes this product law invariant under swapping the two coordinates in any selected pair. Thus for every fixed sign vector $\sigma$, the signed difference process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-f(Z_i'))$ has the same law as the unsigned difference process. Averaging this equality over the finite sign space leaves the right-hand expectation in step 1.1 unchanged when $f(Z_i)-f(Z_i')$ is replaced by $\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-f(Z_i'))$. [F2, F6, F7, step 1.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: For every outcome, put $A:=\max_f|\sum_i\sigma_i f(Z_i)|$ and $B:=\max_f|\sum_i\sigma_i f(Z_i')|$. The triangle inequality gives $\max_f|\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-f(Z_i'))|\le A+B$. Monotonicity and convexity yield $\Phi(A+B)\le\tfrac12\Phi(2A)+\tfrac12\Phi(2B)$; since $A$ and $B$ have the same distribution, the resulting expectation is $\mathbb E\Phi(2A)$. Combining with steps 1.1 and 2.1 proves the desired inequality for finite $\mathcal F_0$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: Enumerate the countable class and let $\mathcal F_k$ be its first $k$ members. The finite-class inequality applies to every $\mathcal F_k$. Its suprema increase to the corresponding suprema over $\mathcal F$. A finite convex function is continuous on $(0,\infty)$; at zero, if $a>0$ and $t\downarrow0$, monotonicity and convexity give $\Phi(0)\le\Phi(ta)\le(1-t)\Phi(0)+t\Phi(a)$, so it is right-continuous there as well. Hence [F5] passes both nonnegative expectations to the limit. A countable subclass giving the same suprema proves the stated separable-version extension. [F1, F5, step 3.1, given] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Use the experiment with data space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$, parameter set $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, and sampling law $P_{\mu,\sigma^2}=N(\mu,\sigma^2)^{\otimes n}$. Let $n\ge2$, $\sigma>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be the independent coordinates of the observation. Define
$$\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2,\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
The map $x\mapsto\bar x$ is a statistic. The sample mean $\bar X$ and residual sum $S^2$ are independent,
$$\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-1}^2,\qquad S>0\ \text{almost surely},\qquad \widetilde T:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-1}.$$
For every $0<\alpha<1$, the interval
$$\left[\bar X-q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n},\ \bar X+q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n}\right]$$
has exact coverage $1-\alpha$, where $q_{n-1}(u)$ is the unique $u$-quantile of $t_{n-1}$ established in [[lem-student-t-and-f-cdfs-are-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]].

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: By [A2], Countable Choice holds, so [F2] applies to the linear continuous map $x\mapsto\bar x$; hence it is a statistic on the stated Borel data space. Put $Z_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma$. The affine pushforward definition in [F1] gives each $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$, and [F1] preserves their independence. Thus $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ by [F4]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F4]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Define $\bar Z=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i$, $u=n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^T$, and $P=uu^T$. Since $u^Tu=1$, $P$ is a rank-one orthogonal projection. We have $u^TZ=\sqrt n\,\bar Z$ and $X-\bar X(1,\ldots,1)^T=\sigma(I_n-P)Z$. Therefore $\bar X=\mu+\sigma u^TZ/\sqrt n$ and $S^2=\sigma^2\|(I_n-P)Z\|^2/(n-1)$. [step 1.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: By [F3], $PZ$ and $(I_n-P)Z$ are independent and $Q:=\|(I_n-P)Z\|^2\sim\chi_{n-1}^2$. The continuous linear map $z\mapsto u^Tz$ is Borel by [A2] and [F2], and $u^TZ=u^TPZ$; the continuous squared-norm map on the complementary vector is likewise Borel. Thus $G:=u^TZ$ and $Q$ are measurable functions of the independent vectors in [F3], so they are independent by [F1]. By [F4], $G\sim N(0,1)$. [A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra, step 2.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: The formulas in step 2.1 express $\bar X$ as an affine function of $G$ and $S^2$ as $\sigma^2 Q/(n-1)$. Hence $\bar X$ and $S^2$ are independent, $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2=Q\sim\chi_{n-1}^2$, and $S>0$ almost surely by [F5]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F5, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.5.1: The set $\{S>0\}$ is Borel and the displayed quotient is continuous there; assigning $0$ on $\{S=0\}$ therefore makes $\widetilde T$ measurable. Since $S=0$ exactly when $Q=0$, step 2.1 gives $\widetilde T=G/\sqrt{Q/(n-1)}$ on $\{Q>0\}$ and both versions are $0$ on $\{Q=0\}$. The variables $G$ and $Q$ are independent with laws $N(0,1)$ and $\chi_{n-1}^2$, so [F5] gives $\widetilde T\sim t_{n-1}$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F5, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.6.1: Let $q=q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)$. By [F5], the $t_{n-1}$ CDF is continuous and symmetric, so $F_{t_{n-1}}(0)=1/2<1-\alpha/2$ and strict increase gives $q>0$; symmetry then gives $F_{t_{n-1}}(-q)=\alpha/2$. Step 5.1 therefore gives $\mathbb P(-q\le\widetilde T\le q)=1-\alpha$. On the full-probability event $\{S>0\}$ from step 4.1, this event is exactly $\{\mu\text{ lies in the displayed interval}\}$ by multiplying by $S/\sqrt n$ and rearranging. The events agree almost surely, so the interval has exact coverage $1-\alpha$. [F5, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

Let $m\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ be fixed, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite class of real-valued functions on their domain. For each $i$, let $\Phi_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\Phi_i(x)-\Phi_i(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, with a common $L\ge0$. Then

$$\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))\le L\,\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F).$$

Equivalently, the unnormalized left expectation is at most $L$ times the unnormalized one-sided supremum on the right.

The same holds for a countable class when both suprema are finite for every sign vector. No condition $\Phi_i(0)=0$ is required; additive constants cancel because the proof compares coordinate differences.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: First fix a coordinate $k$ and condition on all other signs. Put $a_f:=\sum_{i\ne k}\sigma_i f(z_i)$ and $x_f:=f(z_k)$. Averaging over $\sigma_k$ gives $\mathbb E_{\sigma_k}\sup_f(a_f+\sigma_k\Phi_k(x_f))=\frac12\sup_{f,g}(a_f+a_g+\Phi_k(x_f)-\Phi_k(x_g))$. The Lipschitz bound makes the last summand at most $L|x_f-x_g|$. Because ordered pairs include both $(f,g)$ and $(g,f)$, the supremum with $L|x_f-x_g|$ equals the supremum with $L(x_f-x_g)$: swap the pair whenever $x_f<x_g$. Factoring this last supremum gives $\frac12\sup_f(a_f+Lx_f)+\frac12\sup_g(a_g-Lx_g)=\mathbb E_{\sigma_k}\sup_f(a_f+\sigma_k Lx_f)$. [given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: The inequality in step 1.1 holds for every fixed setting of the other signs. Integrating those signs therefore shows that replacing $\Phi_k(f(z_k))$ by $Lf(z_k)$ cannot decrease the expected supremum. Apply this replacement successively for $k=m,m-1,\ldots,1$; each stage keeps all other coordinates fixed and yields $\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_f\sum_i\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))\le L\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_f\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)$. Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$ be finite. For each $i\le n$, let
$(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ be a measurable space and let $P_i,Q_i$ be probability
measures on it. On the finite product measurable space set
$$P=\bigotimes_{i=1}^nP_i,\qquad Q=\bigotimes_{i=1}^nQ_i.$$
With the KL convention of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]],
$$D(P\|Q)=\sum_{i=1}^nD(P_i\|Q_i),$$
where a sum with an infinite term is $+\infty$.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: If $P_i\not\ll Q_i$ for some $i$, choose $A_i\in\mathcal A_i$ with $Q_i(A_i)=0<P_i(A_i)$. The product rectangle $E=X_1\times\cdots\times A_i\times\cdots\times X_n$ has $Q(E)=0$ and $P(E)=P_i(A_i)>0$ by [F2, F3]. Hence $P\not\ll Q$, so the left side is $+\infty$; the corresponding term on the right is also $+\infty$ and the equality holds. [A1, F2, F3, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.1.2: Now suppose $P_i\ll Q_i$ for every $i$, and choose nonnegative representatives $r_i=dP_i/dQ_i$. Define $r(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n r_i(x_i)$, a nonnegative measurable function on the finite product. Repeated Tonelli and the rectangle formulas give $\int_E r\,dQ=\prod_{i=1}^n\int_{A_i}r_i\,dQ_i=\prod_{i=1}^nP_i(A_i)=P(E)$ for every measurable rectangle $E=\prod_iA_i$; applying the same calculation to the full space gives $\int r\,dQ=1$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: The measure $r\,dQ$ is a probability measure by [F4] and step 1.2. The product rectangles form a generating pi-system and the finite product spaces are sigma-finite, so [F3] and the rectangle identity in step 1.2 imply $r\,dQ=P$ on the entire product sigma-algebra. Therefore $r=dP/dQ$ as a Radon–Nikodym class. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.2]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Each $r_i$ is finite $Q_i$-almost everywhere because $\int r_i\,dQ_i=1$, and $P_i(\{r_i=0\})=\int_{\{r_i=0\}}r_i\,dQ_i=0$; thus $0<r_i<\infty$ $P_i$-almost everywhere. Therefore [F6] gives $\log r=\sum_{i=1}^n\log r_i(x_i)$ $P$-almost everywhere. Each $\log r_i$ has integrable negative part by [F1], and the negative part of their finite sum is bounded by the sum of those negative parts. Split each summand into positive and negative parts: Tonelli factors each nonnegative part through the product law, and Fubini applies to the negative parts, which are integrable. Hence, allowing $+\infty$ for positive parts, $\int\log r\,dP=\sum_{i=1}^n\int\log r_i\,dP_i=\sum_{i=1}^nD(P_i\|Q_i).$ By [F1] and step 2.1 the left side is $D(P\|Q)$, proving the claim. [A1, F1, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,Q)$ be a probability space, let $1\le r<\infty$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty VC-subgraph class of measurable real functions with finite VC index $V$. Suppose a measurable envelope $F$ satisfies $|f(x)|\le F(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, and

$$0<\|F\|_{Q,r}:=\left(\int F^r\,dQ\right)^{1/r}<\infty.$$

For every $0<\epsilon<1$, put $K_0:=3e^2/(e-1)$ and $K:=4K_0$. Then

$$N\!\left(\epsilon\|F\|_{Q,r},\mathcal F,L^r(Q)\right)\le\left[K(2/\epsilon)^r\log\!\left(3e(2/\epsilon)^r\right)\right]^{V-1}\le\left(\frac{A}{\epsilon}\right)^{ArV},\qquad A:=12eK+2.$$

The exponent in the first bound is the finite-r logarithmic form. No Axiom of Choice or Countable Choice is used in this proof.

current_proof_step_anchors.1.1: Put $M:=\int F^r\,dQ=\|F\|_{Q,r}^r$. By [F8] $F^r$ is measurable; the hypotheses give $0<M<\infty$. By [F7], the density $F^r/M$ is measurable. Define $R$ by $dR=(F^r/M)\,dQ$; its total mass is one by [F4]. [F4, F7, F8, given, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.2.1: Set $\delta:=\epsilon^r/2^{r+1}$. Then $0<\delta<1$, so [F9] supplies an integer $J\ge1$ with $1/J\le\delta$. Use the grid $U_J$ and probability $\nu_J$ of [F6], and form the product probability $\widetilde Q:=R\otimes\nu_J$ on $\mathcal X\times U_J$ using [F5]. [F5, F6, F9, given, algebra, step 1.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.3.1: Let $X_+:=\{x:F(x)>0\}$ and define $A_f:=\{(x,u):x\in X_+,\ uF(x)<f(x)\}$ for $f\in\mathcal F$. The coordinate projections are measurable because their preimages of measurable sets are rectangles; hence [F7] makes $X_+$ and each $A_f$ product-measurable. On $X_+\times U_J$, the map $\psi(x,u):=(x,F(x)u)$ is injective and $A_f=\psi^{-1}(C_f)$. If a finite set of pairs is shattered by $\{A_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$, its image under $\psi$ is a same-size set shattered by $\{C_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$. Thus the nonempty set class $\mathcal C_J:=\{A_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$ has finite VC index $V_J\le V$. [F1, F7, given, step 2.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.1: Fix $f,g\in\mathcal F$. For $x\in X_+$, put $a(x):=\min(f(x),g(x))/F(x)$ and $b(x):=\max(f(x),g(x))/F(x)$. The envelope gives $-1\le a(x)\le b(x)\le1$, and the section $(A_f\triangle A_g)_x$ is exactly $\{u\in U_J:a(x)\le u<b(x)\}$. By [F6], its $\nu_J$-mass differs from $|f(x)-g(x)|/(2F(x))$ by at most $1/J$. The set $X\setminus X_+$ has $R$-measure zero, since the density $F^r/M$ vanishes there. [F6, F8, step 1.1, step 3.1, given]
current_proof_step_anchors.4.2: Apply [F3] to $\mathcal C_J$ under $\widetilde Q$ at radius $\delta$. Since $e>1$, $K_0=3e^2/(e-1)>1$, and $\delta<1$ makes $\log(3e/\delta)>1$; thus the bracketed base is greater than one, so $V_J\le V$ yields $N(\delta,\mathcal C_J,L^1(\widetilde Q))\le\left[K_0\delta^{-1}\log(3e/\delta)\right]^{V-1}<\infty$. Choose a cover with this many centers $A_{g_1},\ldots,A_{g_k}$, each represented by some $g_j\in\mathcal F$. The cover uses finitely many centers, so this uses only finite choice. [F3, F12, given, choose, step 2.1, step 3.1]
current_proof_step_anchors.5.1: Integrating the section estimate under $R$ and using [F5] gives $\left|\widetilde Q(A_f\triangle A_g)-\frac12\int_{X_+}\frac{|f-g|}{F}\,dR\right|\le\frac1J$. For $x\in X_+$, put $a:=|f(x)-g(x)|\le2F(x)$. If $a=0$ the inequality $a^r\le2^{r-1}F(x)^{r-1}a$ is immediate; if $a>0$ and $r>1$, [F8] raises $a\le2F(x)$ to the positive power $r-1$ and multiplication by $a$ gives it; for $r=1$ it is equality. Hence [F2] gives $\|f-g\|_{Q,r}^r\le2^{r-1}M\int_{X_+}\frac{|f-g|}{F}\,dR\le2^rM\left(\widetilde Q(A_f\triangle A_g)+\frac1J\right)$. The last inequality uses the discrepancy bound and the definition of $R$. [F2, F5, F8, F10, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.6.1: For every $f\in\mathcal F$, some center satisfies $\widetilde Q(A_f\triangle A_{g_j})\le\delta$. Steps 5.1 and 2.1 then give $\|f-g_j\|_{Q,r}^r\le2^rM(\delta+1/J)\le2^{r+1}M\delta=\epsilon^rM$. Thus the function class is covered by the same $k$ centers at radius $\epsilon\|F\|_{Q,r}$, and its covering number is no larger than the set covering number in step 4.2. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 4.2, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.7.1: Put $L:=\log(3e(2/\epsilon)^r)$. From $\delta^{-1}=2(2/\epsilon)^r$ and $\log(3e/\delta)=L+\log2\le2L$ (since $3e(2/\epsilon)^r>2$, so $L>\log2$), the base in step 4.2 is at most $4K_0(2/\epsilon)^rL=K(2/\epsilon)^rL$. Since this base exceeds one, step 6.1 proves the first asserted entropy bound. [F11, F12, step 4.2, step 6.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.8.1: Put $\eta:=(\epsilon/2)^r\in(0,1)$. For $u\ge1$, the function $h(u):=u-\log u$ has $h(1)=1$ and $h'(u)=1-1/u\ge0$; the mean value theorem [F11] gives $\log u\le u$. Hence $K\eta^{-1}\log(3e/\eta)\le3eK\eta^{-2}=3eK(2/\epsilon)^{2r}$. Let $A:=12eK+2$. From [F12], $e-1<e$, so $K_0=3e^2/(e-1)>3e>3$ and $K=4K_0>4$. Thus $x:=3eK>1$ and $A/2=6eK+1\ge x$, whence $(A/2)^{2r}\ge x^{2r}\ge x$ because $r\ge1$. This gives $3eK(2/\epsilon)^{2r}\le(A/\epsilon)^{2r}$. [F11, F12, step 7.1, algebra]
current_proof_step_anchors.9.1: The first bound is the step 7.1 base raised to $V-1$. Since $A/\epsilon>1$, $A\ge2$, and $V\ge1$, we have $2r(V-1)\le ArV$. Thus the first bound is at most $(A/\epsilon)^{ArV}$, proving the second inequality. [step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎
